title: docs(spec): align pair-mcp 003 discover-app section with rf2-7tgfk diagnostic ladder (drift from #2120)
description:
PR #2120 (rf2-7tgfk) refined discover-app's failure-reason surface from the single blanket `:runtime-not-preloaded` reason to a 4-rung diagnostic ladder. The new rungs surface in impl + tests + README, but tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/spec/003-Tool-Catalogue.md §discover-app (lines 277-295) still describes only the legacy single reason.

Impl ladder (probe.cljs, conformance fixtures, README §Failure-path diagnostic ladder):

1. `:nrepl-unreachable` — nREPL port-file missing / socket dead.
2. `:build-not-running` — shadow's :active-builds doesn't include the targeted build; `:running-builds` names the actual ones.
3. `:no-runtime-connected` — build IS running but cljs-eval returns blank (no browser tab, or its ws is dead).
4. `:runtime-loaded-but-preload-missing` — runtime alive, marker absent. Original hint reserved for this rung.

Fallback: `:runtime-not-preloaded` is retained as the degradation case if the ladder itself errors.

Spec/003 currently says only:

> The most common precondition failure on a fresh app is `:reason :runtime-not-preloaded` — the runtime ships into the app via shadow-cljs `:preloads`; the server probes `js/globalThis.__re_frame2_pair_runtime` (the load-time mirror the preload installs) and refuses with a setup hint when missing.

Direction: impl → spec alignment (spec needs to enumerate the 4 new rungs + retain the `:runtime-not-preloaded` fallback). Public-contract surface — consumers (Claude Code, other MCP clients) read the spec to know what failure shapes to expect.

Pre-alpha posture; no shim. Add the rung enumeration as a sub-section under §discover-app naming each `:reason` value + when it fires + hint pattern.

title: re-frame2-pair-mcp: eval-cljs accepts :frame arg
description:
## Why

`eval-cljs` is re-frame2-pair-mcp's escape hatch — when a structured op doesn't cover the question, the programmer evaluates an arbitrary form. Every other structured op (`dispatch`, `snapshot`, `get-path`, `trace-window`, `watch-epochs`, `subscribe`, `reset-frame-db`) accepts a `:frame` arg that targets a named frame. `eval-cljs` doesn't.

So `eval-cljs` runs forms against `:rf/default` by default. `(rf/subscribe [...])` and `(rf/dispatch [...])` inside the supplied form target `:rf/default`. For any multi-frame app — Stories runners, parallel-frame testbeds, micro-frontend islands, counter-per-instance examples, anything using the framework's frame primitive at all — this is silent wrong-frame reads + writes.

Workaround today is wrapping the form manually:

    (rf/in-frame :rf/xray (rf/subscribe [...]))

Easy to forget. When forgotten, the probe targets `:rf/default`, reads `:rf/default`'s db, reports back wrong data, and the programmer either spots it (rare) or proceeds with wrong information.

This is a permanent footgun built into the most-used escape-hatch op. Trivial to fix.

## What changes

### `eval-cljs` MCP op accepts optional `:frame` arg

Input args today:
- `:form` — the ClojureScript form to evaluate
- `:build` — build id
- `:await` — whether to await Promise resolution (rf2-xn4f9)
- `:no-eval` — opt-out gate (rf2-a0z0h)

Add:
- `:frame` — optional keyword (frame-id, e.g. `:rf/xray`). When supplied, the form is wrapped in `(re-frame.core/in-frame <frame-id> <form>)` before evaluation.

When omitted, behaviour is unchanged: form evaluates in whatever ambient frame context exists at the call site (which for the MCP server is `:rf/default`).

Implementation: server-side, before sending the form over nREPL, wrap it:

    (re-frame.core/in-frame :rf/xray
      <user-supplied-form>)

That's literally the entire change. No new framework primitive, no new runtime hook.

### Validation

If `:frame` is supplied and is not a registered, non-destroyed frame in the running app, return:

    {:ok? false :reason :unknown-frame :supplied <frame-id> :registered [...]}

Same error shape as the equivalent check on `dispatch`, `snapshot`, etc.

## Acceptance

1. `mcp__re-frame2-pair__eval-cljs` accepts optional `:frame` arg.
2. When `:frame :rf/xray` is supplied, `(rf/subscribe [...])` inside the form reads `:rf/xray`'s reactive graph; `(rf/dispatch [...])` mutates `:rf/xray`'s app-db.
3. When omitted, behaviour is identical to today's (no regression for existing recipes / probes).
4. Unknown `:frame` returns the structured error above, matches other ops' frame-validation shape.
5. Skill documentation updated:
   - `references/ops.md` — `eval-cljs` arg table mentions `:frame`
   - Main skill body §Multi-frame model — note that `eval-cljs` joins the family of frame-aware ops
   - One recipe in `references/recipes.md` showing the pre-vs-post pattern (the manual `(rf/in-frame ...)` wrapping replaced by the arg)
6. mcp-conformance test: `eval-cljs` with `:frame :rf/xray` reads `:rf/xray`'s state, not `:rf/default`'s.

## What does NOT change

- The `eval-cljs` form-evaluation pipeline (still nREPL → CLJS REPL → form eval)
- The `:await` mode (rf2-xn4f9) — composes orthogonally; `(rf/in-frame ...)` wraps a Promise-returning form just fine
- The `:no-eval` opt-out gate (rf2-a0z0h)
- Existing probes / recipes that don't pass `:frame` — unchanged behaviour
- `re-frame.core/in-frame` — already exists; this bead just uses it

## What DOES change

- `eval-cljs` MCP op accepts `:frame` arg
- Skill references updated to describe the new arg
- A class of silent-wrong-frame reads is eliminated for any multi-frame app

## Worker — conduct your own review before starting

title: re-frame2-pair-mcp: dispatch-dry-run op (simulate cascade without commit)
description:
## Why

A re-frame2 programmer wanting to know "if I dispatch X, will it do what I expect?" — schema-pass? fx-fire? sub-recompute? machine-transition? — has no way to ask without committing. Today the pattern is:

1. `snapshot` to capture current state
2. `dispatch` to commit the experiment
3. Inspect what happened (likely via the cascade summary once that lands)
4. `restore-epoch` to roll back
5. Hope no irreversible effects fired (http calls, navigation, persisted writes) — they HAVE — programmer is now in a corrupt state and the experiment cost real money / changed real systems

The "experiment, don't speculate" principle the re-frame2-pair skill teaches is undermined when experimenting is destructive. A dry-run primitive — full cascade computed, fx NOT executed, db rolled back transparently — turns every dispatch into a safe-to-try probe.

Universal across app shapes. "Will adding this item trip the cart schema?" "Will this navigation event leave the route in a valid state?" "Will this form submit fire the right fx?" — all answered without firing the fx.

## What it is

New MCP op: `mcp__re-frame2-pair__dispatch-dry-run`

Input args:
- `:event` — the dispatch vector (same as `dispatch`)
- `:frame` — optional frame-id (same as `dispatch`)
- `:include-machine-cascade?` — default `true` — simulate machine transitions caused by this dispatch
- `:max-effect-chain-depth` — default `1` — for fx that dispatch further events, how deep to simulate (1 = simulate this dispatch's reducer + its direct fx + which events those fx WOULD dispatch, but do not simulate those subsequent events)

Output: same shape as the augmented `dispatch` response (cascade summary), PLUS:
- `:dry-run? true` flag at top level
- `:would-fire-effects` — explicit list of fx that WOULD have executed but did not (with their args, so the programmer can reason about real-world impact)
- `:db-state-after-simulation` — what `app-db` WOULD look like if committed (already in `:cascade :db-diff`, but surfaced as a complete snapshot too for direct inspection)
- `:rolled-back? true` — confirmation that the framework's app-db is unchanged from pre-call state

## How it works

The framework's cascade pipeline already has a clean separation between reducer (pure) + fx execution (side-effectful). Dry-run runs the reducer, computes the would-be `:effects` list, simulates schema validation, runs the machine-step machinery (which is itself pure), captures sub-invalidations and would-be re-renders — but DOES NOT execute fx and DOES NOT commit the resulting db.

Implementation route: a special-purpose internal entry point (`re-frame.core/dispatch-dry-run-internal` or equivalent) that runs the cascade pipeline with the fx-executor stubbed to "collect, don't execute". After computing the cascade summary, the framework discards the proposed db state without committing.

This is NOT the same as snapshot + dispatch + restore-epoch:
- No epoch is recorded (the dry-run does not appear in epoch history)
- No fx execute (snapshot+dispatch+restore would have already fired http/navigation/persisted-writes between steps 2 and 4)
- No watcher / listener fires (sub recomputations are simulated, not commit-triggered)
- No state diff visible to other consumers (Xray panels, other MCP subscribers don't see a phantom epoch)

The result is a TRUE "what would happen" probe.

## Edge cases

1. **Schema violation in dry-run** — fully evaluated. Programmer sees the violation in the cascade summary, can reason about whether the recovery mode would kick in.
2. **Reducer exception in dry-run** — caught, surfaced in cascade summary with exception details. Framework state unchanged.
3. **Machine transitions** — fully simulated; machine snapshot computation is pure data.
4. **`:after` timers** — simulated armings appear in `:would-fire-effects` as `:rf.machine/after-schedule` fx entries. NOT scheduled in real wall-clock; the wall-clock scheduler is fx-side and is stubbed.
5. **Subs that have already been computed in the real graph** — dry-run uses the current sub graph state as input; sub-invalidations are reported but the real sub graph is unchanged.
6. **Cascades that would dispatch further events via fx** — bounded by `:max-effect-chain-depth`. Default 1 means "this dispatch's reducer + its direct fx + which subsequent events would be dispatched (listed, not simulated)". Depth 2 means "and simulate those too". Avoids unbounded cascade simulation.
7. **Frame mismatch** — if `:frame` is unregistered, error `:reason :unknown-frame`. Same handling as `dispatch`.

## Acceptance

1. `dispatch-dry-run` MCP op exists and returns the cascade summary that `dispatch` would have produced, but with `:dry-run? true` + `:rolled-back? true` flags.
2. After a successful dry-run, `snapshot` returns identical state to before the dry-run was called. Verified by a test.
3. After a dry-run with `:would-fire-effects` containing an http fx, no http request was actually made. Verified by a test that mocks the http fx and asserts zero calls.
4. Dry-run honours `:frame` arg — running against `:rf/xray` simulates a cascade in that frame without committing.
5. Dry-run captures schema violations the same way the real cascade does — programmer sees what would fail.
6. `:max-effect-chain-depth` bounds the simulation; depth=1 is the safe-and-cheap default.
7. Dry-run epochs do NOT appear in epoch history (no entry in `(rf/epoch-history frame-id)`).
8. Dry-run does NOT fire `register-listener!` callbacks or `register-epoch-listener!` callbacks.
9. Skill recipe added: "test a dispatch before committing it" — recipe shows the dry-run flow + when to use vs `dispatch`.

## What does NOT change

- `dispatch`, `reset-frame-db`, `restore-epoch` MCP ops — unaffected, dry-run is additive
- Framework cascade pipeline behaviour for real dispatches — unchanged
- Epoch history shape — unchanged (dry-runs simply don't appear there)
- Schema validation, fx routing, machine machinery — same code paths, just with fx-executor stubbed and commit suppressed

## What DOES change

- New MCP op: `mcp__re-frame2-pair__dispatch-dry-run`
- New internal framework entry point for cascade simulation without commit (this is the bigger lift)
- Skill references add a "dry-run" pattern recipe
- Existing recipes that say "snapshot, dispatch, inspect, restore" simplify to "dry-run"

## Worker — conduct your own review before starting

1. Audit the cascade pipeline: is reducer / fx execution / db commit already separated cleanly enough to stub the fx side? If not, that separation work is a precursor (or part of this bead's scope).
2. Determine where in the cascade pipeline schema validation lives — make sure dry-run hits the same validation, not a parallel path that diverges.
3. Identify the machine-step machinery's purity — is it already pure data transformation, or does it have side-effects (scheduling timers, etc.) that need stubbing?
4. Confirm dry-run can be implemented without leaking phantom state into the reactive sub graph. The graph reads existing inputs, computes hypothetical outputs, but the cache isn't updated.
5. Consider whether dry-run should support batched dispatches (a list of events to simulate in order). Probably out of scope for v1; flag as follow-up.
6. State which test surfaces validate dry-run correctness (mcp-conformance + framework cascade tests).
7. Report findings before pushing implementation.

## References

- Spec 009 §Epoch records — what the cascade summary returns
- Spec 005 — state machines (machine-step purity)
- Framework cascade: `implementation/core/src/re_frame/...` (worker — identify the right entry point)
- Companion: dispatch-cascade-summary bead (separate, lands first since dry-run reuses the cascade summary shape)
- Pair-debug session 2026-05-26 — the "experiment without consequences" universal primitive

title: re-frame2-pair-mcp: dispatch/reset/restore return cascade summary
description:
## Why

re-frame2-pair-mcp's primary value-add is letting a programmer ask "I did a thing; what happened?". Today that answer requires correlation across multiple ops:

1. `dispatch` returns `{:ok? true}` — confirmation that the event entered the queue, nothing about what it did
2. Programmer correlates by epoch-id (if they captured one) OR sets up `watch-epochs` BEFORE the dispatch (subscription has to be running)
3. Programmer then runs `snapshot` / `get-path` to see what changed
4. To see effects, separate `trace-window` call

Every probe a programmer writes that has the shape "dispatch X and check Y" pays this multi-call cost. For something as fundamental as "did my dispatch do what I expected?", the chained-call ergonomics are wrong. The information already exists — the epoch-record assembled by the framework is the cascade summary — it's just not surfaced in the response.

Universal across app shapes: counter / form / cart / machine-driven / multi-frame / single-frame all dispatch and all want to know what happened.

## What changes

### `dispatch` MCP op

Augment the response to include the resulting cascade summary as a new top-level key. Today (success):

    {:ok? true :build "<id>"}

After:

    {:ok? true
     :build "<id>"
     :epoch-id <uuid-or-counter>
     :cascade {:db-diff {:path-changes [...] :added [...] :removed [...]}
               :effects [{:fx-id ... :args ... :outcome ... :coord ...} ...]
               :sub-invalidations [{:sub-id ... :paths-affected ...} ...]
               :renders [{:render-id ... :reason ...} ...]
               :machine-transitions [{:machine-id ... :from ... :to ... :phase ...} ...]
               :trace-events [...]}}

The cascade slot mirrors the `:rf/epoch-record` projection shape (Spec 009 §Epoch records) — programmers already familiar with `watch-epochs` see the same shape. Apply the standard wire-size mechanisms (`:rf.mcp/dedup-table`, `:rf.size/large-elided`, `:rf/redacted`) so the response stays within budget.

Failure path: if the cascade threw (reducer exception, schema violation, fx errored), include the cascade as far as it got, the failure reason, AND the final committed state. "What broke + what state am I in?" answered in one call.

### `reset-frame-db` MCP op

Same enhancement — return what changed between pre-reset and post-reset db:

    {:ok? true :cascade {:db-diff {...} :sub-invalidations [...] :renders [...]}}

### `restore-epoch` MCP op

Same — return the diff from current-pre-restore to target-epoch, plus the effects-not-replayed marker (which effects the original cascade fired that CANNOT be undone — http calls, navigation, persisted writes). The programmer needs this surfaced as part of the restore response so they can reason about "what state am I really in?".

    {:ok? true
     :restored-to <epoch-id>
     :cascade {:db-diff {...} ...}
     :unreplayable-effects [{:fx-id ... :original-args ... :reason :side-effect-irreversible} ...]}

## Acceptance

1. `dispatch` MCP op response includes the cascade summary on success AND on cascade-internal failure.
2. Schema for the `:cascade` slot is documented + matches the Spec 009 `:rf/epoch-record` projection shape (operators reading the response don't need to learn a new shape).
3. Wire-size budget honoured: cascades > N bytes are deduped + large-slot-elided per the existing `:rf.mcp/dedup-table` mechanism. Programmer can request full detail via existing knobs (`max-tokens`, `elision`).
4. `reset-frame-db` and `restore-epoch` return parallel `:cascade` summaries. `restore-epoch` additionally surfaces `:unreplayable-effects`.
5. Frame-targeting honoured: when `dispatch :frame :rf/xray` is called, the cascade summary reflects what happened in `:rf/xray`, not in `:rf/default`.
6. Pre-alpha posture: no back-compat shim. Old response shape (`{:ok? true :build ...}` only) is replaced. Consumers (re-frame2-pair skill ops.md, anything in `tools/` reading MCP responses, any tests) are updated in the same PR.
7. The retain-N trace ring buffer is NOT the source — the cascade summary comes from the assembled epoch-record (programmer-facing projection), not the raw trace bus.

## What does NOT change

- The MCP op names (`dispatch`, `reset-frame-db`, `restore-epoch`)
- Their input arg shapes
- The underlying framework primitives (re-frame2 core dispatch / epoch assembly)
- `watch-epochs`, `subscribe`, `eval-cljs`, `get-path`, `snapshot`, `trace-window` — unaffected
- The wire-size budget mechanisms (programmers still tune via `max-tokens`, `elision`, etc.)

## What DOES change

- `dispatch`, `reset-frame-db`, `restore-epoch` MCP op responses each gain a `:cascade` slot
- `restore-epoch` additionally gains `:unreplayable-effects`
- Skill references (`ops.md`, `recipes.md`, `wire-size-budget.md`) updated to describe the new response shape
- Any existing recipes that say "dispatch then watch-epochs to see what happened" are simplified to a single call

## Worker — conduct your own review before starting

1. Confirm the framework already assembles an epoch-record on every cascade (Spec 009). If not, this bead needs a precursor bead for that.
2. Audit the existing MCP server's `dispatch` op — is it `await`ing the cascade today, or returning before completion? If returning before completion, the cascade summary needs an explicit await step. This may interact with the `:await true` mode added by rf2-xn4f9 — confirm it composes.
3. Identify which cascade-summary fields are cheap to compute vs expensive. The expensive ones (full trace events) should be elided by default and opt-in via existing wire-size knobs.
4. Verify the `:rf/epoch-record` shape covers everything programmers need. If `:machine-transitions` aren't in the standard projection, add them (the assembled trace already has them; just thread through).
5. State which test surfaces validate the new response shape (mcp-conformance, re-frame2-pair-mcp tests).
6. Report findings before pushing implementation.

## References

- Spec 009 §Epoch records — the existing projection shape
- Wire-size mechanisms: `references/wire-size-budget.md`
- Existing MCP server: `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/`
- Pair-debug session 2026-05-26 — the universal "what happened?" question this primitive answers

```bash
git -C C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2 log --since='24 hours ago' --pretty='%h %s' main
```

Approximate set (~29 PRs):
- Per-frame trace rings: #2135 (spec) + #2139 (impl) + #2140 (Tool-Pair drift fix) + #2141 (consumer adoption)

## Method

For each PR (rebase-merged, so the merge commit is the impl artefact):

1. Walk `git show <merge-commit> --stat` and identify (a) what spec it should align to, (b) what spec it actually touches.
2. For each impl file touched, check whether the spec section that contracts it was updated in the same PR. If not, check whether the prior spec already covered the new behaviour (= already aligned) OR whether the spec drifted (= file a bead).
3. For each spec file touched, check whether the impl matches verbatim. If the spec describes a contract the impl hasn't fully landed, file a bead.

   - `spec/009-Instrumentation.md` ↔ `implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace/` (huge per-frame trace ring work)

   - `spec/005-StateMachines.md` § Guards / § After-transitions ↔ pending rf2-82a0u changes when it lands
   - `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/spec/003-Tool-Catalogue.md` ↔ pair-mcp impl
   - `tools/story-mcp/spec/Principles.md` ↔ story-mcp impl

## Deliverables

- **Per drift found:** one new bead with:
  - title `docs(spec): align <spec-file> with <impl-area> drift from <PR#>`
  - body: quote both sides verbatim; identify which direction the alignment goes (spec → impl or impl → spec); whether back-compat shims are needed (no — pre-alpha)
  - priority: P2 if a public contract is involved, P3 if internal-only doc drift
- **Per false alarm:** a one-line note in the audit summary (which surfaces were checked + found clean).
- **Summary report** in the audit bead's notes: which PRs audited, surfaces checked, findings count.

## Out of scope

- Code changes (this bead is audit-only; file derived beads for any impl/spec fixes).
- PRs older than 24h.
- ai/findings/ docs (local-only; cannot be audit subjects from committed view).

Default to **JVM** read for spec / impl cross-check (faster + grep-friendly). No tests need to pass for this bead — it produces text artefacts (beads + a summary).

title: feat(machines): trace enhancements for Xray Handler section — :phase on action-ran, :threw on guard-evaluated, standardised :rf.machine.timer/cancelled with :reason
description:
## Why

The epoch panel's Handler section (designed in `ai/findings/epoch-panel-handler-section-design.md`) needs to render machine-handler cascades richly: TRANSITION, GUARDS, LIFECYCLE (phase-grouped: exit / transition / entry), AFTER TIMERS, DATA REDUCTION, SNAPSHOT DIFF, FX with per-action attribution.

Re-audit of `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/` (pair-debug session 2026-05-25) confirms most of the data needed is already emitted — including `:rf.machine.timer/scheduled` (arming), `:rf.machine.timer/fired` (timer fire), `:rf.machine.timer/stale-after`, `:rf.machine.timer/skipped-on-server`, and all guard/action/snapshot/spawn events. Three real gaps remain that force the panel into either spec-walk-at-render-time (brittle, slow, breaks on hot-reload mid-render) or invisible-failure (guard exceptions vanish from the trace).

Pre-alpha posture: no back-compat shims. Existing consumers (current Xray rendering, re-frame2-pair-mcp, external monitors) are updated as part of this bead to consume the new shapes; legacy event ids are deleted. Goal is elegance + correctness, not preservation of legacy surfaces.

## Three enhancements

### 1. `:rf.machine/action-ran` — add `:phase` field

Current emit (`transition.cljc:658`):

    (trace/emit! :rf.machine :rf.machine/action-ran
                 {:machine-id parent-id
                  :action-id  action-ref
                  :input      {:data (:data snap) :event event}
                  :outcome    (if (nil? r) :ok r)
                  :frame      frame-id})

Add `:phase` — a closed-set keyword identifying which lifecycle slot the action came from:

    :exit              ; from an exited state's :exit slot
    :transition        ; from the matched transition's :action(s)
    :entry             ; from an entered state's :entry slot
    :always            ; from an :always-transition's action
    :after-action      ; from an :after-transition's action
    :initial-entry     ; from build-initial-snapshot's entry cascade
    :destroy-exit      ; from destroy-time exit cascade (re-frame.machines.lifecycle-fx.exit-cascade)

`collect-actions` already knows which list it's iterating; thread the phase keyword through from its callers (`apply-transition-once`'s four cascade phases — exit / transition / entry / spawn — already have named pure helpers per `transition.cljc:1109`-1316).

Same change required at the destroy-time exit path (`lifecycle_fx/exit_cascade.cljc:88`) and the initial-entry path (build-initial-snapshot's seed cascade) so every action-ran emit carries `:phase`.

### 2. `:rf.machine/guard-evaluated` — capture `:threw` outcome

Current emit (`transition.cljc:142`):

    (trace/emit! :rf.machine :rf.machine/guard-evaluated
                 {:machine-id (or (:rf/parent-id machine) (:id machine))
                  :guard-id   guard-ref
                  :input      {:data (:data snapshot) :event event}
                  :outcome    (if outcome :pass :fail)
                  :frame      (:rf/frame machine)})

Current `evaluate-guard` (`transition.cljc:131`-154) has NO try/catch around `(call-guard g snapshot event)`. If a guard throws, the exception propagates up and **the trace emit is bypassed entirely** — the operator sees neither the guard evaluation nor its failure mode.

Add `:threw` to the outcome closed set + an `:exception` slot:

    (defn- evaluate-guard
      [machine guard-ref snapshot event]
      (if (nil? guard-ref)
        true
        (let [g (resolve-guard machine guard-ref)]
          (try
            (let [outcome (boolean (call-guard g snapshot event))]
              (trace/emit! :rf.machine :rf.machine/guard-evaluated
                           {:machine-id (or (:rf/parent-id machine) (:id machine))
                            :guard-id   guard-ref
                            :input      {:data (:data snapshot) :event event}
                            :outcome    (if outcome :pass :fail)
                            :frame      (:rf/frame machine)})
              outcome)
            (catch #?(:clj Throwable :cljs :default) e
              (trace/emit! :rf.machine :rf.machine/guard-evaluated
                           {:machine-id (or (:rf/parent-id machine) (:id machine))
                            :guard-id   guard-ref
                            :input      {:data (:data snapshot) :event event}
                            :outcome    :threw
                            :exception  e
                            :frame      (:rf/frame machine)})
              ;; Spec 005 §Guards — a throwing guard is treated as :fail
              ;; (transition doesn't match); the trace surfaces the exception
              ;; for operator diagnosis, the engine continues searching.
              false)))))

Closed outcome set after this change: `:pass / :fail / :threw`.

The engine's existing fail-on-throw semantics for guards (treat throw as `:fail` and skip this transition candidate) are preserved — only the trace gains the missing event + exception context. Confirm exact behaviour against Spec 005 §Guards before landing; if spec says guard-throw should abort the whole cascade rather than treat as :fail, mirror that.

### 3. `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled` — single event, all cancellation paths, with `:reason`

Today only `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled-on-resolution` exists (`timer.cljc:205`), covering one cancellation path. Other cancellation paths (state exit, machine destroy, transition supersede, frame destroy) either don't emit or use different/missing event ids.

Standardise on one event in the existing `:rf.machine.timer/` namespace covering every path:

    (trace/emit! :rf.machine :rf.machine.timer/cancelled
                 {:machine-id machine-id
                  :state      state-owning-the-timer       ; matches :scheduled's :state shape
                  :delay      resolved-delay-ms
                  :epoch      scheduled-epoch              ; matches :scheduled's :epoch
                  :reason     reason                       ; closed set, see below
                  :frame      frame-id})

Closed set of reasons:

    :on-exit            ; state owning the :after was exited by a transition
    :on-destroy         ; machine was destroyed (lifecycle.destroy or finalize)
    :on-resolution      ; timer fired AND resolution happened
                        ;   (the existing :cancelled-on-resolution case)
    :on-supersede       ; new transition re-entered the owning state, replacing the timer
    :on-frame-destroy   ; the machine's frame was destroyed

Payload shape mirrors `:rf.machine.timer/scheduled` (existing arm event) for symmetry — same `:machine-id` / `:state` / `:delay` / `:epoch` / `:frame` slots — so the panel can pair scheduled→fired→cancelled by `(machine-id, state, epoch)`.

**Delete `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled-on-resolution`** — replaced wholesale by `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled` with `:reason :on-resolution`. Pre-alpha posture: no alias, no transition window; the new event id is the only event id.

Audit each cancellation site, ensure each emits with the right `:reason`:
- `timer.cljc:205` migrates from `cancelled-on-resolution` → `cancelled` with `:reason :on-resolution`
- The transition engine's exit path (when an exited state had armed timers) emits `:reason :on-exit`
- The destroy-time exit cascade emits `:reason :on-destroy`
- Frame-destroy emits `:reason :on-frame-destroy`
- The transition engine's supersede path (re-entering an `:after`-bearing state) emits `:reason :on-supersede`

## What this unlocks

The Handler section's machine-handler render becomes:

    ;; LIFECYCLE rendering — phase-grouped from a single filter
    (group-by :phase
              (filter #(= :rf.machine/action-ran (:event-id %))
                      epoch-trace-events))

    ;; AFTER TIMERS rendering — arm/fire/cancel paired by (machine-id state epoch)
    (let [armed     (filter #(= :rf.machine.timer/scheduled (:event-id %))
                            epoch-trace-events)
          fired     (filter #(= :rf.machine.timer/fired (:event-id %))
                            epoch-trace-events)
          stale     (filter #(= :rf.machine.timer/stale-after (:event-id %))
                            epoch-trace-events)
          cancelled (filter #(= :rf.machine.timer/cancelled (:event-id %))
                            epoch-trace-events)]
      ;; pair into rows by (machine-id state epoch) for the panel
      ...)

    ;; GUARD failure attribution
    (filter #(and (= :rf.machine/guard-evaluated (:event-id %))
                  (= :threw (:outcome %)))
            epoch-trace-events)

Direct, fast, spec-independent. No spec walking at render time.

## Acceptance

1. Every `:rf.machine/action-ran` emit carries `:phase` from the closed set above. No emit site missed — audit destroy-time exit cascade (`lifecycle_fx/exit_cascade.cljc:88`) + initial-entry cascade (build-initial-snapshot's seed) + the four `apply-transition-once` phases.
2. `:rf.machine/guard-evaluated` captures throws as `:outcome :threw` with `:exception` slot. The engine's existing fail-on-throw semantics for guards are preserved (per Spec 005 §Guards); only the trace gains the missing event.
3. Every `:after` timer cancellation — across every cancellation path — produces an `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled` trace with `:reason` set to the appropriate closed-set value. Audit each cancellation site to confirm coverage.
4. `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled-on-resolution` is **deleted**. Existing consumers are migrated to `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled` with `:reason :on-resolution`. Single canonical event id; no legacy alias.
5. Consumers updated as part of this bead: Xray's current panels that read cancellation events, re-frame2-pair-mcp's trace projection (if it filters on the old event id), any tests asserting against the old event id. Pre-alpha posture — clean cut, not parallel surfaces.
6. The epoch panel's Handler section (per `ai/findings/epoch-panel-handler-section-design.md`) can render LIFECYCLE (phase-grouped), AFTER TIMERS (arm + fire + cancel with reasons + stale), and GUARDS (with throws first-class) directly from the trace stream — no spec walking at render time.
7. Test coverage: pure-data conformance tests pin the new emit shapes; one regression test per cancellation path verifies the corresponding `:reason` fires; one regression test per guard-throw scenario verifies `:outcome :threw` + `:exception` ride the trace; the old event id `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled-on-resolution` must not appear anywhere in source post-change.

## What does NOT change

- Macrostep emit (`:rf.machine/transition`), microstep emit (`:rf.machine.microstep/transition`), snapshot emit (`:rf.machine/snapshot-updated`), event-received emit, spawn emits, lifecycle emits — all unchanged shape
- Existing timer arm event (`:rf.machine.timer/scheduled`) — unchanged; provides the "armed" signal the panel needs
- Existing timer fire events (`:rf.machine.timer/fired` with `:fired? true/false`, `:rf.machine.timer/stale-after`, `:rf.machine.timer/skipped-on-server`) — unchanged
- `:rf.machine/after-schedule` fx — unchanged; keeps doing the wall-clock scheduling work
- Public API of `reg-machine` — unchanged

## What DOES change

- `:rf.machine/action-ran` payload gains `:phase` (every emit site, no exceptions)
- `:rf.machine/guard-evaluated` payload gains `:threw` outcome path + `:exception` slot (try/catch added around `call-guard`)
- `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled` is new + covers every cancellation path
- `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled-on-resolution` is deleted
- Consumers of the deleted event id are updated

## Out of scope (potential follow-up beads)

The audit also surfaced two gaps that aren't blocking the panel design but are worth noting:

- **Raise tracing** — successful raises (`(raise ...)` inside an action) emit no trace; only `:rf.error/machine-raise-depth-exceeded` does. Operator can't see the internal raise cascade. Worth a `:rf.machine/raise-emitted` event eventually; not needed for this panel iteration.
- **Transition source-coord** — `:rf.machine/transition` carries machine-id but not the source-coord of the specific `:on` / `:after` slice that matched. The panel can jump to the machine's `reg-machine` site but not to the matched transition's source line. Worth adding `:source-coord` to the macrostep emit eventually; current rendering can fall back to "open the machine spec; navigate manually".

## Worker — conduct your own review before starting

Before writing any code, do an independent audit and report back:

1. **Re-verify the gap list.** Walk `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/` yourself. List every `trace/emit!` and `trace/emit-error!` call you find. Cross-reference against the "What does NOT change" section above to confirm the bead's understanding of existing emissions is correct.
2. **Check guard-throw semantics against Spec 005 §Guards.** This bead assumes the engine's intent is fail-on-throw → treat as `:fail` → continue evaluating other transition candidates. Confirm in the spec. If the spec says guard-throw should abort the cascade (different semantic), the trace handling differs — surface the discrepancy before implementing.
3. **Audit cancellation paths exhaustively.** This bead lists five reasons (`:on-exit`, `:on-destroy`, `:on-resolution`, `:on-supersede`, `:on-frame-destroy`). Walk the source and confirm these are the complete set. If you find a sixth cancellation path, propose adding it to the closed-set before implementing.
4. **Sanity-check the panel design's claim.** Read `ai/findings/epoch-panel-handler-section-design.md`'s §Trace stream section. Confirm the gap analysis matches your audit. If the panel design depends on data this bead doesn't surface, raise it.
5. **Identify any over-engineering.** This bead's pre-alpha posture wants elegance + correctness, not parallel surfaces or alias preservation. If any acceptance criterion looks like a back-compat shim or unnecessary parallel surface, push back.
6. **Spec touchpoints.** Spec 005 (§Trace events, §Guards) and Spec 009 (§Instrumentation) need updating to reflect the new emit shapes. List the specific sections you'll touch.

Report your findings in a comment on the bead (or in the PR description) before pushing implementation code. If your audit agrees with the bead's understanding, say so explicitly so the reviewer knows you confirmed rather than skipped. If you disagree on any point, surface it for resolution before writing code — a fix to a bead's specification is much cheaper than a fix after the implementation is half-done.

## Investigation hints for the worker

- Four named phases in `apply-transition-once` (`transition.cljc:1109`-1316) — exit-phase, transition-phase, entry-phase, spawn-phase — are pure helpers. Threading `:phase` through `collect-actions`'s caller surface is the right hook point.
- `evaluate-guard` at `transition.cljc:131`-154 is the only guard-call site under the main engine; wrap `call-guard` in try/catch + emit the `:threw` outcome on catch. Verify against Spec 005 §Guards whether the engine should still treat throw as `:fail` (current implicit behaviour via propagation) or abort the cascade — mirror whichever the spec says.
- For `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled` standardisation: walk all uses of `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled-on-resolution`, all `interop/cancel-after!` call sites, all `:rf.machine/after-cancel` fx handler invocations, all places where snapshot mutations invalidate prior timers (the `:rf/spawn-counter` bumps). Each is a cancellation path; each needs the new event with the right `:reason`.
- The destroy-time exit cascade (`lifecycle_fx/exit_cascade.cljc`) needs BOTH the action-ran `:phase :destroy-exit` AND `:rf.machine.timer/cancelled :reason :on-destroy` for any `:after` timers active in the configuration being destroyed.

## References

- Trace audit details: `ai/findings/epoch-panel-handler-section-design.md` §Trace stream — what's already emitted vs what the panel needs
- Guard emit + missing throw path: `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/transition.cljc:131`-154
