title: audit(performance): tools/story
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

- `tools/story` is a Storybook-class playground for re-frame2 variants and workspaces, with most real runtime cost concentrated in the interactive dev/test shell rather than end-user app paths.
- The main steady-state work is variant execution (`run-variant`), shell rerendering, controls editing, trace capture/projection, and optional watch-mode auto-reruns.
- Production app impact is intentionally low because the slice is compile-time gated by `re-frame.story.config/enabled?`; static Story builds still run the shell, but skip the 500ms hot-reload poll when `static-mode?` is true.

## Likely hot paths

- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/runtime.cljc:136-183,360-399` — `run-loaders!`, `run-events!`, `run-variant`.
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/shell.cljs:71-147,174-180` — fingerprint poll and watch-mode hash poll.
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/identity.cljc:131-147,192-247` — canonicalisation and snapshot hashing.
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/controls.cljs:206-253,505-535` — arg resolution, argtype/schema derivation, recursive widget rendering during edits.
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/sidebar.cljs:372-416` and `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/state.cljc:355-366,543-560` — registry snapshot, filtering, grouping, sorting, testable-set derivation.
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/trace.cljs:64-68,109-119,274-350` — bounded trace buffering and regrouping.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Dev/JVM is the important case here: polling, trace listeners, recorder, scrubber, docs, and run-all tests are all active.
- CLJS production app builds should mostly elide this slice through `enabled? false`, so the main risk is degraded developer UX, slower tests, or slower static Story pages, not shipping app latency.
- Static Story builds are still performance-sensitive, but they already avoid the always-on poll via `static-mode?`.

## Findings

- `ui/shell.cljs` does steady polling work even before watch mode is enabled. `compute-fingerprint-snapshot` walks every running variant every 500ms, and watch mode adds `compute-testable-content-hashes`, which re-hashes every testable variant on the same cadence.
- The watch-mode hash path is the clearest scalable hotspot. `identity/snapshot-identity` resolves args and canonicalises/sorts/`pr-str`s the tuple for each variant, so cost grows with variant count and args/schema size, not just with visible UI work.
- `ui/controls.cljs` does duplicate work on every edit. `args-editor` resolves effective args, then `resolve-argtypes` performs its own registry/schema walk and calls `args/resolve-args` again for fallback inference. This is a likely typing-latency hotspot.
- `ui/sidebar.cljs` rebuilds a full registry-derived view model on each shell-state render: snapshot, tag filtering, grouping, sorting, and testable-set computation. `test-widget` separately recomputes `testable-variant-ids`. Acceptable at small scale, but likely the next dev-time drag as the registry grows.
- `ui/trace.cljs` re-groups the retained buffer on every buffer or scrub change, but the 200-event cap keeps this bounded. I would not prioritize changes here yet.
- The explicit hot-path commentary is good in `runtime.cljc`, `ui/shell.cljs`, and `ui/trace.cljs`. It is weaker in `ui/controls.cljs` and `ui/sidebar.cljs`; if those paths are optimized, add comments marking them as rerender/keystroke hot paths.

## Recommended changes

- Highest ROI: make watch-mode hash recomputation incremental. Recompute only for changed variants, or only when registrar state / active modes / substrate actually changed, instead of on a blind 500ms full scan.
- Make the controls path single-pass. Pass precomputed `eff-args` into `resolve-argtypes`, or split argtype derivation into a static per-variant schema/argtypes phase plus a cheap dynamic fallback for unresolved keys.
- In the sidebar, compute `testable-variant-ids`, `testable-set`, grouped variants, and visible tags once per render and pass them down. Deeper memoization can wait until registry size justifies it.
- Leave trace projection alone for now. If it later shows up in profiling, memoizing `group-cascades` by buffer identity should be enough; a broader redesign is not justified yet.

## Spec impact

None

## Commands checked

- `bd prime`
- `git status --short`
- `rg --files tools/story`
- `Get-ChildItem tools/story/src/re_frame/story -Recurse -File | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object Length,FullName`
- `rg -n "reg-sub|sort-by|group-by|reduce|reduce-kv|mapv|filter|keep|distinct|snapshot-identity|sha|digest|doseq|for|concat|flatten|into|vals|frequencies" ...`
- `Get-Content` and line-numbered `Get-Content` on the files listed below

## Files checked

- `tools/story/README.md`
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story.cljc`
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/config.cljc`
- `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/runtime.cljc`

title: audit(performance): tools/mcp-conformance
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

- `tools/mcp-conformance` is dev/CI-only tooling: Node MCP end-to-end checks plus JVM Malli/grep conformance checks for shared wire vocabulary.
- There is no prod app/runtime path here; any cost matters only to local iteration and CI wall time.
- Measured here: `tools/mcp-conformance/wire-vocab` passed `28` tests / `437` assertions in about `4356 ms`. `test/end-to-end-causa.js` skipped in about `52 ms`.
- The other Node entrypoints were not runnable in this workspace without installing `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`.

## Likely hot paths

- Repeated source/spec reads and repeated string stripping in the JVM conformance suite:
  `wire-vocab/test/re_frame/mcp_conformance/fixtures.clj`,
  `wire_vocab_test.clj`,
  `slot_name_test.clj`,
  `indicator_field_test.clj`.
- Hermetic live-overflow orchestration:
  `scripts/run-live-pair2-overflow-hermetic.cjs` does fixture dependency install, `shadow-cljs` boot, HTTP/nREPL polling, headless Chromium launch, and then forks the live test.
- End-to-end Node tests are dominated by child-process startup and server handshake, especially the JVM-backed `end-to-end-story.js`.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Prod: none. This slice is isolated test tooling.
- Dev/CI: cold-start cost dominates. The biggest costs are JVM startup, `shadow-cljs`/browser boot, and repeated file I/O in the wire-vocab suite.
- The hermetic path is intentionally expensive and already heavily commented. The repeated file-scan path is cheaper per operation but happens on every wire-vocab run.

## Findings

- Medium: `read-source` is a plain `slurp` with no caching in `wire-vocab/test/re_frame/mcp_conformance/fixtures.clj:70-77`, and the test namespaces call it repeatedly inside `doseq` scans over the same files (`wire_vocab_test.clj:571-656`, `760-920`; `slot_name_test.clj:331-454`; `indicator_field_test.clj:250-375`). This is the clearest slice-local overhead that can be reduced without changing behavior.
- Low: `strip-comments-and-strings` in `fixtures.clj:106-160` is linear and reasonable, but it is also re-run against the same source text across multiple tests. Memoizing the stripped result by file path would remove duplicate CPU work.
- Low: The repeated-scan path is not commented as an intentional simplicity tradeoff. If it stays uncached, add a short comment saying startup dominates and the team is deliberately avoiding extra caching complexity.
- Low: `scripts/run-live-pair2-overflow-hermetic.cjs:378-550` is wall-time heavy by design, but the cost is overwhelmingly external process orchestration, not slow in-process JS. I would not add complexity here unless CI timing shows this job is materially hurting throughput.
- Low: `package.json` runs the Node scripts sequentially. Given CI already fans these checks out by job and local runs are mostly startup-bound, parallelizing the local script probably is not worth the coordination/debugging cost.

## Recommended changes

- Memoize `read-source` by relative path in `wire-vocab/test/re_frame/mcp_conformance/fixtures.clj`.
- If that lands, also memoize `strip-comments-and-strings` on top of the cached file contents.
- If no caching is added, put a short comment near `read-source` or the larger grep loops documenting that repeated reads are a deliberate simplicity tradeoff.
- Leave the hermetic runner shape alone unless CI measurements show it is a meaningful bottleneck.

None

title: audit(performance): tools/mcp-base
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

- `tools/mcp-base` is a small CLJC shared library for `pair2-mcp`, `story-mcp`, and planned `causa-mcp`.
- It is not on the app render/event path directly. It sits on the MCP wire boundary: arg coercion, sensitive filtering, epoch diffing, elision counting, and response token capping.
- The busiest real caller today is likely `pair2-mcp` in dev-style sessions. `story-mcp` is JVM-side and lower-frequency, but large responses still pay the same tree-walk costs.

## Likely hot paths

- `tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/diff_encode.cljc`: `collect-map-patches`, `diff-encode-db-after`, and `validate-patches!` on epoch slices.
- `tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/sensitive.cljc`: `strip-sensitive` and `scrub-snapshot` on trace and epoch batches.
- `tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/elision.cljc`: `count-elided-markers` on already-shaped payload trees.
- `tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/cap.cljc`: `sum-text-tokens` and `apply-cap` on every `tools/call` result.
- `args.cljc`, `overflow.cljc`, and `vocab.cljc` are ubiquitous but cheap enough that they do not justify extra complexity without profiling.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Dev is the higher-risk mode here. `pair2-mcp` runs these helpers in repeated snapshot reads, epoch/history reads, and subscription drains (`tools/pair2-mcp/src/re_frame_pair2_mcp/tools/wire_pipeline.cljs:81-85,112-115`, `tools/pair2-mcp/src/re_frame_pair2_mcp/tools/subscribe.cljs:160-162`).
- `pair2-mcp` ships as a Node `:simple` shadow-cljs build today, not an `:advanced` build, so CLJS-only compile-time elision opportunities are not currently doing much by default.
- JVM consumers keep Malli validation on unconditionally, so diff-encode validation cost is present there too.
- "Prod" cost in this slice is mostly payload-size-dependent, not QPS-dependent: large app-db / epoch / trace payloads dominate over helper parsing.

## Findings

1. The slice's real cost is repeated full-data passes, not tiny helper overhead. In the live pair2 pipeline, the same logical payload can go through sensitive scrub, diff encode, dedup, elision count, and token count before egress. Within this slice, `sensitive`, `diff_encode`, `elision`, and `cap` are the only functions worth treating as hot.
2. `re-frame.mcp-base.sensitive/strip-sensitive` always allocates a fresh vector on the default path even when nothing is dropped (`tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/sensitive.cljc:46`). The docstring says the common path is cheap, but the current `filterv` form rebuilds the vector anyway. On subscription drains and snapshot scrubs, where sensitive records should usually be rare, that is avoidable churn.
3. `re-frame.mcp-base.diff-encode/validate-patches!` is a real steady-state cost on the diff hot path, not just a theoretical dev-only guard (`tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/diff_encode.cljc:143`). The code supports CLJS compile-time disablement, but the checked `pair2-mcp` build does not set that closure define and uses `:optimizations :simple`; JVM consumers always validate. Every epoch diff therefore pays both the diff walk and a full Malli validation walk.
4. `re-frame.mcp-base.elision/count-elided-markers` is intentionally simple and correctly centralized, but it is still a full post-hoc tree walk over the payload about to be shipped (`tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/elision.cljc:37`). On large snapshot/app-db responses, this is likely the next-most-expensive slice-local pass after diff encoding.
5. Hot-path commentary is already strong. `cap`, `diff_encode`, `sensitive`, and `elision` all explain ordering and performance posture clearly enough that I would not add more comments unless the `strip-sensitive` docstring stays out of sync with the implementation.
6. I found no benchmark or perf harness in this slice. The test surface is behavioral only. `clojure -M:test` passed: 89 tests, 223 assertions, 0 failures.

## Recommended changes

- Change `strip-sensitive` to a single-pass fast path that returns the original vector when `dropped-count` is zero, and only allocates a transient result after the first dropped item. This is the clearest slice-local win.
- Make diff-patch validation explicitly build-config-driven instead of implicitly "available but usually on". At minimum, decide whether shipped `pair2-mcp` builds should set `re-frame.mcp-base.diff-encode/validate-patches? false`; keep it on in tests.
- Do not add more passes to this library unless the win is large. If elision counting becomes measurable, the right fix is to surface the count from the upstream elision producer instead of micro-optimizing `count-elided-markers`.
- Leave `args`, `overflow`, and `vocab` alone. They are centralized, simple, and unlikely to move any meaningful latency or allocation number.

## Spec impact

None.

## Commands checked

- `bd prime`
- `Get-ChildItem -Force tools/mcp-base`
- `rg --files tools/mcp-base/src`
- `rg --files tools/mcp-base/test`
- `rg --files tools/mcp-base/spec`
- `Get-Content tools/mcp-base/deps.edn`
- `Get-Content` on the files listed below
- `rg -n` over slice and consumer call sites for `strip-sensitive`, `scrub-snapshot`, `count-elided-markers`, `diff-encode-epochs`, `apply-cap`, `parse-*`, `validate-patches?`, and `closure-defines`
- `rg -n "criterium|benchmark|bench|perf" tools/mcp-base/src tools/mcp-base/test tools/mcp-base/spec`

title: audit(performance): tools/causa-mcp
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

- `tools/causa-mcp` is spec-only today: `README.md` plus `spec/`, with no `src/`, `test/`, or shipped runtime in this slice.
- The intended runtime is a long-lived Node stdio JSON-RPC server with one persistent shadow-cljs nREPL socket and a browser-side injected runtime.
- In the planned design, steady-state cost is not process startup. It is repeated `cljs-eval` round-trips plus payload shaping at the wire boundary.

## Likely hot paths

- `subscribe`: drain subscription queues, filter sensitive events, elide large values, optionally dedup, emit `notifications/progress`, then reschedule.
- Large read tools: `get-trace-buffer`, `get-epoch-history`, `get-app-db`, `get-app-db-diff`, and `get-machine-state`.
- The wire pipeline on tree- and sequence-shaped responses: path slicing, summary/sample/full projection, pagination, dedup, elision, and rendered-size measurement against `max-tokens`.
- Dev-only polling: `tail-build` repeatedly re-evaluating a probe until hot reload lands.
- Cheap by design and worth keeping cheap: `discover-app`, `list-subscriptions`, `list-tools`, and `session-info`.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Dev is the higher-risk mode for call frequency: hot reloads, `tail-build`, live trace subscriptions, repeated introspection, and runtime sentinel probes.
- Prod-like sessions are more about payload size than call count: deep app-db reads, epoch history, and long-lived trace/error/fx streams.
- Because this slice is spec-only, there is no current prod cost to fix. The main value here is avoiding an expensive retrofit when implementation lands.

## Findings

1. There is no present in-slice runtime hot spot yet. Any recommendation beyond the already-specified socket reuse and wire-budget posture would be premature complexity.
2. The biggest guaranteed performance win is already locked in: one persistent nREPL socket. Reconnect-per-call would be a hard regression for both latency and streaming support.
3. The future hot path is the wire boundary, not tool registration. Repeated tree walks and serialization on trace/app-db/epoch tools will dominate over local dispatch scaffolding.
4. There is a contract drift risk around streaming granularity. `tools/causa-mcp/spec/004-Wire-Pipeline.md` says one event per `notifications/progress`, but `tools/causa/spec/010-MCP-Server.md` still describes batch emission, and the analogous `pair2-mcp` `subscribe` implementation is batch-per-drain. Copying that code verbatim would violate the slice spec and change the cost profile.
5. `list-subscriptions` is correctly scoped as a small request/response diagnostic. It should not inherit heavier pagination or dedup machinery unless real data shows unusually large subscription counts.
6. The analogous `pair2-mcp` hot paths are well-commented, but this slice has no implementation yet. When `tools/causa-mcp/src/` lands, comments should be added on wire-pipeline ordering, the streaming poll loop, and any cap-measurement shortcut paths; those are subtle hot paths where unmarked refactors are likely to regress behavior or cost.

## Recommended changes

- Keep the future implementation simple and centralised: one shared wire-pipeline helper, not per-tool inline shrink logic.
- Reuse the proven cheap wins from `pair2-mcp`: cached default build-id lookup, persistent socket reuse, one `swap!` per stream drain, and early runtime-side filtering/elision before large values cross nREPL.
- Resolve the streaming contract before implementation. If `subscribe` is truly per-event, do not port `pair2-mcp`'s batch tick shape unchanged.
- Treat `tail-build` as dev-only and keep its polling conservative; it should not drive prod-oriented architecture decisions.
- Do not add extra caching, hashing, or digest computation by default. The significant wins here are pagination, summary modes, elision, and socket reuse; more machinery is only justified after real traces show a bottleneck.

None.

description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

`tools/machines-viz` is currently a spec-only slice. It defines a future dev-tool CLJS artifact: `MachineChart`, a static read-only viewer, share-URL encode/decode, and PNG/SVG export. There is no executable implementation in this slice today; `tools/causa` still carries a placeholder and explicitly notes that `tools/machines-viz` does not exist yet as code.

## Likely hot paths

- Chart layout and topology normalization on mount, registry change, and compound expand/collapse. This is the main structural cost once implemented.
- Live overlay updates from `[:rf/machines <id>]` plus `:rf.machine/*` traces: active-state pulse, transition glow, microstep flash, timer state, and spawned-child updates.
- `:after` countdown rings at 60Hz when visible. In multi-chart dev screens, this is the clearest CPU hot path.
- `:invoke-all` rows and spawned-child trays, which combine trace churn with structural DOM/layout churn.
- `:auto-pan?` on transition, if implemented naively, because it can force extra layout reads/writes and scroll work.
- Export/share flows are bursty rather than steady-state hot, but PNG at 2x DPR and EDN -> transit -> base64url can still spike CPU and memory on large charts.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- By spec, this slice is dev-only and should stay out of application production bundles via tool classpath isolation and upstream `debug-enabled?` gating.
- The standalone viewer is still a real runtime surface, so hot-path discipline matters even though normal app prod bundles should not include this tool.
- The stress case is dev: Story variant grids, Causa embeds, hot reloads causing registry changes, and multiple visible charts with live timers.

## Findings

- No runtime code exists in `tools/machines-viz` yet, so there is no current hot path to measure. This audit is necessarily spec-driven.
- The highest-risk future regression is coupling live snapshot/trace updates to full graph recompute. The spec already says layout must not rerun on every transition; the implementation needs to preserve that separation explicitly.
- The visible-only 60Hz `:after` ring rule is correct, but it is also the most obvious place to burn CPU if each chart or ring gets its own timer/loop.
- `:invoke-all` and spawned-child rendering are the next most likely dev hot paths because they combine high event volume with structural updates.
- None of these hot paths are commented in code yet, because there is no code. When implementation lands, add comments at the layout invalidation boundary and the animation/update loop.

## Recommended changes

- Keep topology/layout state separate from runtime highlight state so transitions, microsteps, and timer updates can change attrs/classes without rebuilding or re-laying out the graph.
- Use one chart-level, visibility-gated animation clock for `:after` rings and pulse effects, not per-node timers.
- Treat layout invalidation rules as load-bearing and comment them in code: recompute only on registry change and expand/collapse.
- Keep export/share implementation simple until measured. The current spec and the existing `>8KB` fallback are enough for v1.
- If multi-chart embeds prove heavy, lean on the existing `:show-microsteps?`, `:show-after-rings?`, `:show-invoke-all?`, and `:show-spawned?` props before adding more complex caching.

title: audit(performance): tools/causa
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile
`tools/causa` is a dev-only, in-app debugging overlay that preloads listeners in dev builds, keeps its own 1000-event trace ring, and mounts the UI lazily on first open (`tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/preload.cljs`, `mount.cljs`, `trace_bus.cljc`).

Steady-state cost is mostly dev-only and comes from two places: the always-on trace collector (`trace_bus.cljc:96-141`) and, once the shell is open, panel composites over the shared trace/app-db/epoch surfaces (`registry.cljs:100-134`). Prod cost is intended to be elided behind `interop/debug-enabled?`; the real risk in this slice is dev INP, DOM mount count, and duplicate dev-memory retention.

## Likely hot paths
- `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/trace_bus.cljc:96-141` `collect-trace!`: runs on every emitted trace in dev.
- `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/registry.cljs:125-134` `:rf.causa/cascades`: shared `projection/group-cascades` pass over the whole retained buffer.
- `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/panels/app_db_diff.cljs:545-554` `:rf.causa/selected-epoch-diff` plus `app_db_diff_helpers.cljc:100-183` `diff-paths`: recursive diff over host app-db snapshots.
- `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/panels/trace_helpers.cljc:263-288`, `issues_ribbon_helpers.cljc:339-360`, `mcp_server_helpers.cljc:336-354`: feed builders that rescan the full retained buffer while their panels are active.
- `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/panels/hydration_debugger.cljs:468-504`: full hydration composite; currently also kept live indirectly by the shell sidebar.
- `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/panels/causality_graph.cljs:340-374` plus `causality_graph_helpers.cljc:111-246,321-367`: enrich, project, and lay out the entire visible graph.

## Dev vs prod considerations
- Prod should not ship this slice at all; `preload.cljs:107-113` gates side effects on `interop/debug-enabled?`, and the README states the surface is dev-only.
- Dev still pays trace capture even before the shell is opened, because preload-time registration happens immediately and the Causa-side ring is separate from the framework ring (`trace_bus.cljc:1-27`, `preload.cljs:4-23`).
- The largest user-visible risks are therefore dev-only: too many mounted rows, repeated whole-buffer projections while panels are open, and expensive app-db diffs against large host states.
- The existing perf test file checks algorithmic invariants, but it does not verify actual DOM row-cap enforcement in the views (`tools/causa/test/day8/re_frame2_causa/perf_budget_cljs_test.cljc:11-31`).

## Findings
1. High: the stated `<= 200` row/dispatch render budget is not explicitly enforced across several long-list surfaces.
   `tools/causa/test/day8/re_frame2_causa/perf_budget_cljs_test.cljc:13-18` and `:88-98` treat `200` rows / dispatches as a hard contract, but `trace.cljs:398-403`, `issues_ribbon.cljs:372-377`, `mcp_server.cljs:464-469`, `performance.cljs:276-281`, `event_detail.cljs:293-300`, `subscriptions.cljs:242-249`, `effects.cljs:196-203`, and `flows.cljs:177-184` all render whole vectors. `causality_graph_helpers.cljc:220-246` also intentionally does not cap dispatch count, and `trace_bus.cljc:18-22,65-68` only caps raw events at `1000`, which is not equivalent to “last 200 dispatches.” `machine_inspector.cljs:263-309` shows the intended capped-list pattern, but most other panels do not use it.
2. High: App-db diff recomputes the full diff instead of caching it, despite comments saying it is cached.
   `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/panels/app_db_diff.cljs:539-544` says the selected-epoch diff is cached per `:epoch-id`, but `:rf.causa/selected-epoch-diff` just calls `h/diff-paths` directly on every recompute (`app_db_diff.cljs:545-554`). `diff-paths` itself is well-structured and benefits from structural sharing, but it still does recursive key-union work over changed subtrees (`app_db_diff_helpers.cljc:147-183`). On large host app-dbs, this is the most likely user-visible slowdown in the slice.
3. Medium: the dormant hydration badge keeps an expensive detail composite live while the shell is open.
   `tools/causa/src/day8/re_frame2_causa/shell.cljs:184-190` subscribes to `:rf.causa/hydration-debugger-data` only to read `:has-mismatch?`, but that composite also builds the mismatch summary, resolves selection, computes divergence detail, and builds hash-chip paths (`hydration_debugger.cljs:468-504`, `hydration_debugger_helpers.cljc:330-365`). That work is unnecessary unless the Hydration panel is actually open.
4. Low: some hot-path comments are inaccurate or incomplete and should be corrected if the code stays as-is.
   `trace_helpers.cljc:238-240`, `issues_ribbon_helpers.cljc:313-315`, and `mcp_server_helpers.cljc:310-312` describe their feed builders as “one pass,” but the implementations reproject/filter and then do additional axis/count passes (`trace_helpers.cljc:264-276`, `issues_ribbon_helpers.cljc:340-358`, `mcp_server_helpers.cljc:337-353`). `app_db_diff.cljs:539-544` also claims a cache that does not exist. These are active paths when the relevant panels are open, so the comments should either match reality or call out the deliberate tradeoff.

## Recommended changes
- Enforce explicit row caps or virtualization at the panel boundary for long lists. Start with Trace, Issues, MCP, Performance, Event Detail, and any list that can grow with retained trace history. Reuse the `machine_inspector.cljs` `cap-transitions` pattern or promote a shared `cap-rows` helper.
- Enforce the causality-graph’s `200`-dispatch budget directly on cascades/nodes before layout, instead of relying on a `1000`-event ring to approximate it.
- Add a real per-epoch diff cache for `:rf.causa/selected-epoch-diff`, bounded to the retained epoch history. This added complexity is justified here because app-db size can dominate every other slice input.
- Split hydration presence from hydration detail. The shell sidebar should subscribe to a cheap boolean/count sub; only the Hydration panel should build `mismatch-detail`.
- After caps land, only then consider collapsing the Trace / Issues / MCP feed builders into fewer passes if profiles still show them hot. The missing caps and uncached diff are higher-value fixes.
- Fix or add hot-path comments where behavior is currently misleading, especially around row caps, hydration’s always-live sidebar dependency, and the nonexistent app-db diff cache.

## Spec impact
None

title: audit(performance): implementation/ssr-ring
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

`implementation/ssr-ring` is a synchronous Ring host adapter around the SSR runtime. Its steady-state cost is entirely request-driven: `ssr-handler` creates a per-request frame, runs the synchronous `:on-create` drain, reads the resolved SSR response, renders HTML, builds the hydration payload, materialises headers/cookies, and destroys the frame. Construction-time work (`validate-handler-opts!`, default merging) is not hot.

## Likely hot paths

- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring.clj:115` `ssr-handler`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/pipeline.clj:27` `setup-request-frame!`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/pipeline.clj:66` `build-full-response`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/response.clj:10` `ssr-response->ring-response`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/headers.clj:27` `headers->ring-map`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/cookie.clj:53` `cookie->set-cookie-header` when many cookies are emitted

The real request-time weight is `build-full-response`: SSR render, render-hash generation, payload serialisation (`pr-str`), route head resolution, and HTML shell assembly.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Dev overhead is higher because per-request frame create/destroy still emits trace traffic, and SSR/head failures are routed through warning/error tracing.
- Prod latency scales mostly with rendered tree size and hydration payload size. `:payload-keys` is the main built-in control for keeping payload serialisation and wire size down.
- Custom `:html-shell` and route `:head` code run on every successful request. If callers do template parsing, disk reads, or other avoidable work there, that will dominate adapter-local costs.
- `:emit-hash? false` currently avoids only the hash done inside `render-to-string`; payload hash generation still happens.

## Findings

- Significant: successful HTML requests do duplicate render-tree hashing. In `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/pipeline.clj:83-86`, `build-full-response` calls `ssr/render-to-string` and then separately calls `ssr/render-tree-hash`. Upstream, `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/emit.cljc:225-246` already computes `hash/render-tree-hash` inside `render-to-string` when `:emit-hash?` is true to stamp `data-rf-render-hash`. On the default path that is two full canonicalisation/hash passes over the same hiccup tree per request.
- Minor: non-redirect HTML responses collapse header pairs twice. `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/headers.clj:56` builds a Ring header map just to check for content-type, then `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/response.clj:10` rebuilds the header map for the actual response.
- Expected but important: payload serialisation is linear in the selected app-db slice (`implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/pipeline.clj:87-92`). That is not a defect, but it means callers that omit `:payload-keys` on large request dbs will pay for it on every request.

Hot-path commentary is generally good in this slice. The duplicate-hash path is not called out as a latency-sensitive double traversal; if it remains, a short comment should be added there.

## Recommended changes

- Highest value: remove the duplicate hash pass. Add an internal SSR helper that returns both rendered HTML and the render hash, or thread a precomputed hash into `render-to-string`, then reuse that single hash for both the DOM attribute and payload `:rf/render-hash`.
- Low priority: fold content-type defaulting into response materialisation, or replace `ensure-content-type`'s full map build with a cheap case-insensitive scan of header pairs.
- Documentation only: add a brief note near `build-full-response` or the `:payload-keys` option that payload size is directly on the request hot path.

## Spec impact

None

## Commands checked

- `bd prime`
- `rg --files implementation/ssr-ring`
- `Get-ChildItem -Recurse implementation/ssr-ring/src,implementation/ssr-ring/test`
- `rg -n "^(\\(defn|\\(defn-)" implementation/ssr-ring/src implementation/ssr-ring/test`
- `rg -n "TODO|FIXME|NOTE|perf|performance|hot path|hot-path|cache" implementation/ssr-ring/src implementation/ssr-ring/test`
- `Get-Content` on the slice source/test files and selected upstream SSR/core files
- `rg -n` against upstream SSR/core functions referenced by the slice
- `clojure -M:test` in `implementation/ssr-ring` (`24` tests, `102` assertions, `0` failures, `0` errors)

## Files checked

- `implementation/ssr-ring/deps.edn`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring.clj`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/cookie.clj`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/handler_defaults.clj`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/headers.clj`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/lifecycle.clj`
- `implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/payload.clj`

- Read-only upstream context: `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/emit.cljc`, `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/hash.cljc`, `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/head/emit.cljc`, `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/head/registry.cljc`, `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/error_listener.cljc`, `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/request.cljc`, `implementation/core/src/re_frame/frame.cljc`

title: audit(performance): implementation/ssr
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

`implementation/ssr` owns the SSR request/response path for re-frame2: server-side `render-to-string`, optional structural render hashing for hydration, per-request request/response side-channel state, hydration checks, error projection, and head/meta HTML emission.

The dominant steady-state server path is:

1. Create a server frame.
2. Populate `request-slots`.
3. Drain app logic.
4. Render body HTML via `re-frame.ssr.emit/render-to-string`.
5. Optionally compute `data-rf-render-hash`.
6. Read `response-slots` via `get-response`.
7. Destroy the frame and clear per-frame side channels.

The dominant client-side path in this slice is first-render hydration verification (`verify-hydration!`), not ongoing interaction.

## Likely hot paths

- `re-frame.ssr.emit/render-to-string` and `emit-element`: recursive tree walk, registered-view resolution, tag parsing, attr emission, escaping, child string assembly.
- `re-frame.ssr.hash/render-tree-hash`: full-tree canonicalisation plus FNV pass when `:emit-hash?` is enabled, and again on the client for `verify-hydration!`.
- `re-frame.ssr.response/*`: per-request `:rf.server/*` fx accumulation, especially header replacement/appends on redirect/login-style responses.
- `re-frame.ssr.request/on-frame-destroyed!`: per-request teardown swaps for request, response, pending error traces, and head snapshots.
- `re-frame.ssr.head.registry/render-head` and `re-frame.ssr.head.emit/head-model->html`: usually once per request, so warm but not primary.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Dev-only or dev-heavy cost is mostly in error/detail surfaces: `:dev-error-detail?`, extra warning/error traces, and tooling-oriented source-coord annotation.
- Prod server cost is mostly body rendering plus optional render hashing. If a host does not enable `:emit-hash?`, the slice is materially cheaper.
- Client hydration cost is boot-time only, but large trees pay the same structural hash cost again in `verify-hydration!`.
- Head/meta emission and error projection should stay simple unless profiles show otherwise; they are not the main steady-state server hotspot today.

## Findings

- `render-to-string` with `:emit-hash? true` is the clearest production multiplier. `render-to-string` computes `render-tree-hash` first, then does a separate HTML emit. `render-tree-hash` itself builds a full canonical EDN string and then walks that string again in `fnv-1a-32`. That is an extra whole-tree allocation/traversal on a request path that can absolutely be live in prod.
- The slice's built-in slow load test is healthy right now. `clojure -M:test -n re-frame.ssr-teardown-load-test` passed at about 9.6k req/s for 2,000 requests, with no leaked frames/slots and about 1.64 MB total heap delta (about 857 bytes retained per request). The request/response side-channel design and teardown path do not currently look like the bottleneck.
- A one-off in-process benchmark of a 200-row registered-view tree showed a median of about 565.8 ms for 500 renders without hashing vs about 646.1 ms with `:emit-hash? true` (about 14 percent slower). That is noisy and not a substitute for a real profiler, but it matches the code shape: hashing is not free and is paid on top of emission.
- `emit-element` is the other real hot loop. It does a registry lookup for every keyword-headed vector, regex tag parsing for every DOM tag, and string materialisation for every child sequence. The file is well commented about semantics, but the repeated lookup/parse/allocation cost in this loop is not called out explicitly; if this path is touched, hot-path comments should be added there.
- `response/replace-header` is linear in header count and lower-cases names repeatedly, but response header vectors are usually tiny. It is not worth complicating unless a real profile shows unusually header-heavy workloads.
- Head/meta and error projection paths are not urgent performance targets. `render-head`/`head-model->html` are typically once per request, and error projection is only paid on error paths.

## Recommended changes

- Highest value: keep the hash output identical, but change `render-tree-hash` from `canonical-edn` string materialisation plus a second byte pass to a single streaming walker/hash writer. This is the one recommendation here with clear hot-path upside in both server SSR and client hydration.
- Low-risk follow-up: add a small cache around `parse-tag-name` results in `re-frame.ssr.emit`. Repeated HTML tags are common, and this avoids paying regex/split/join work on every emit.
- Only after measuring again: if body render still dominates after hash work, inspect `emit-element` for cheaper DOM-tag fast paths or less child-string intermediate allocation. Do not add complexity here blind.
- Do not complicate `request`/`response` teardown or header bookkeeping yet. The current load result says those paths are already acceptable.
- If `emit-element` or header mutation code is optimised, add explicit hot-path comments near that logic so future edits do not quietly reintroduce allocation-heavy work.

## Spec impact

None

## Commands checked

- `bd prime`
- `git status --short`
- `rg --files implementation/ssr`
- `rg -n ... implementation/ssr/src/... implementation/ssr/test/...`
- `Get-Content implementation/ssr/deps.edn`
- `clojure -M:test -n re-frame.ssr-teardown-load-test`
- `clojure -M -` with an inline benchmark comparing `rf/render-to-string` with and without `:emit-hash?`

## Files checked

title: audit(performance): implementation/http
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile
- `implementation/http` implements the managed HTTP slice: request shaping, per-frame middleware, in-flight tracking and aborts, retry/backoff, decode/accept, privacy-aware trace emission, and the machine/test wrapper surface.
- The real wall-clock cost is usually network I/O, but the local CPU/allocation path is `managed-handler -> run-attempt! -> handle-response! -> decode-response-body`.
- CLJS production can dead-code-elide most trace/privacy work behind `interop/debug-enabled?`. JVM cannot: `implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.clj:105` sets `debug-enabled?` to `true`, so trace/privacy overhead remains live there.

## Likely hot paths
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_handlers.cljc:81` and `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_transport.cljc:414` run for every managed request, with `run-attempt!` re-running on retries.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_encoding.cljc:51`, `:73`, and `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_decode.cljc:124` cover query merging, body encoding, and success-path decoding.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/util_json.cljc:164` and, on JVM without Cheshire, `:34` are the JSON parse/stringify path.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_registry.cljc:243` resolves actor ownership on each request.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_middleware.cljc:115` is on the request path when apps register interceptors.
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_privacy.cljc`, `http_privacy_headers.cljc:80`, and `http_url.cljc:95` are on the trace path in CLJS dev and JVM.

## Dev vs prod considerations
- CLJS prod: trace emission and most privacy redaction work are effectively free after DCE.
- CLJS dev: privacy/header/query redaction is active and can matter in request-heavy local sessions.
- JVM/test/SSR: trace emission is always enabled, so "dev-only" privacy and trace shaping are runtime costs worth auditing.

## Findings
- Repeated denylist merging is the clearest avoidable allocation source. `http_privacy_headers.cljc:80-105` and `http_url.cljc:95-101` rebuild `set/union` on every header/query-param lookup, and the walkers call those predicates once per entry. This is minor per request, but it compounds across all traced HTTP traffic and matters on JVM because traces stay live.
- The JVM JSON fallback is the biggest likely hot spot when Cheshire is absent. `util_json.cljc:34-175` falls back to a pure Clojure parser/writer for successful JSON responses and JSON request bodies. That is fine as a compatibility path, but it is much more allocation-heavy than Cheshire/native parsing and sits directly on the success path.
- `http_registry/compute-actor-id` (`http_registry.cljc:243`) is the only always-on non-I/O path here with input-size-sensitive work. It derefs app-db (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/frame.cljc:169`) and scans `:rf/spawned`. The existing fast path for "no spawned actors" is good, but machine-heavy apps can still pay an O(size of spawned registry) walk per request.
- I did not find a strong case for extra complexity in `merge-params`, `encode-body`, `content-type-of`, retry backoff math, or the current registry `swap!` counts. Those costs are small relative to network I/O and decode/trace work.
- The JVM JSON fallback is on a real hot path but is not explicitly called out in-code as a slow fallback. If it remains, that comment should be added.

## Recommended changes
- Replace repeated `set/union` membership checks with either direct `(or (contains? default k) (contains? @extra k))` checks or a cached merged denylist recomputed only on mutation. This is low complexity with clear benefit on every traced request.
- Treat Cheshire as the expected JVM production dependency for this slice, or emit a one-time warning when the fallback parser/writer is active. Optimizing the handwritten fallback itself is probably not worth the complexity unless Cheshire-free JVM production is a deliberate goal.
- Leave `compute-actor-id` alone unless profiling in a machine-heavy app shows it as a real cost. If it does show up, the right fix is a reverse lookup / explicit actor-id threading strategy, not smaller loop micro-optimizations.
- Keep interceptor chains shallow and request interceptors cheap. If an app leans heavily on middleware, document that it is part of the request hot path.

## Spec impact
None

## Commands checked
- `bd prime`
- `rg --files implementation/http`
- `Get-ChildItem -Recurse implementation/http/src/re_frame/*.cljc`
- `Get-Content` on the slice source files and selected core files
- `rg -n` searches for hot-path functions and debug/trace gates
- Inspection only; no tests or benchmarks were run

## Files checked
- `implementation/http/deps.edn`
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http.cljc`
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_managed.cljc`
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_handlers.cljc`
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_transport.cljc`
- `implementation/http/src/re_frame/http_registry.cljc`

title: audit(performance): implementation/flows
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile
`implementation/flows` implements optional, frame-scoped computed-state flows that run after each `:db` commit and before `:fx` (`implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:182-202`, `implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc:374-384`).

Steady-state cost is dominated by post-drain `run-flows!` for frames with registered flows. Registration, clear, and hot-reload invalidation live in `registry.cljc` and are usually cold by comparison. The artefact split already keeps apps with no flows from paying any of this slice.

## Likely hot paths
- `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:182-202` `run-flows!`: runs after every committed drain; loops all flows in the frame.
- `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:80-180` `read-inputs` / `evaluate-flow!`: repeated `get-in`, dirty-check `=`, `assoc-in`, and `swap! last-inputs`.
- `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/topo.cljc:110-174` `topo-sort`: re-runs on every drain and every registration.
- `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:108-179` flow trace emission: `:skip`, `:computed`, and `:failed` all sit on the drain path; `:computed` / `:failed` also run `elide-wire-value`.
- `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc:158-203` `reg-flow`: `topo-sort` on the prospective map for every registration / hot reload.
- `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc:239-305` `clear-flow`: app-db read/write plus O(frame-count) registrar retention check.

`topo.cljc` is already explicit about hot-path tradeoffs. `evaluate-flow!` is also a hot path, but its trace-payload work is not called out as performance-sensitive in the same way.

## Dev vs prod considerations
- CLJS prod: `trace/emit!` is gated on `interop/debug-enabled?` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc:441-460`), but its arguments are still evaluated before the function call. This slice therefore still pays tag construction unless the call site adds its own outer gate.
- JVM / SSR / tests: `re-frame.interop/debug-enabled?` is `true` on CLJ (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.clj:105`), so flow trace work is always live there.
- Dev hot reload: `invalidate-flow-on-replace!` is cheap O(1) because `last-inputs` is keyed by flow-id first (`implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/registry.cljc:315-328`).
- Core already uses outer call-site gating for trace work in other hot areas (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/registrar.cljc:137-148`), so this slice currently diverges from the prevailing pattern.

## Findings
1. High: `evaluate-flow!` eagerly builds trace payloads on the post-drain hot path even when tracing is disabled.
   `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:139-151` and `:170-179` call `elision/elide-wire-value` before `trace/emit!` can short-circuit. Because `trace/emit!` is a function, not a macro, CLJS prod still evaluates those arguments. Dirty flows that touch large nested values will still pay the walk in prod, even though no trace is emitted.
2. Medium: every drain recomputes topological order from a static per-frame graph.
   `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:193` calls `topo/topo-sort` every time. `topo.cljc` documents why this is acceptable for small registries, so this is not a correctness bug, but it is the next likely steady-state CPU sink if flows become common or frames carry more than a handful of nodes.
3. Low: skip traces allocate on every unchanged drain pass.
   `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc:101-112` emits `:rf.flow/skip` for every stable flow on every drain. The per-call cost is small, but it scales with `flows * drains`; in CLJS prod the tag map is still built unless the call site is outer-gated.
4. Low: `evaluate-flow!` is a real hot path, but the code does not explicitly warn future editors to keep trace payload construction debug-gated and cheap.

## Recommended changes
- Add outer `when interop/debug-enabled?` gates around flow trace call sites in `implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc`, and move `elide-wire-value` work inside the gated branch. This is low-complexity and likely the highest-value change in this slice.
- Add one short hot-path comment near `evaluate-flow!` / the trace blocks stating that this code runs after every drain and must not build trace payloads unless debug is enabled.
- Do not add topo-order caching yet. Measure real per-frame flow counts and drain frequency first. If profiles show `topo-sort` materially expensive, cache ordered ids per frame and invalidate only on `reg-flow` / `clear-flow`.
- Leave `clear-flow`'s O(frame-count) registrar retention scan alone unless multi-frame production profiles actually show it.

## Spec impact
None

## Commands checked
- `bd prime`
- `rg --files implementation/flows`
- `Get-Content implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows.cljc`
- `Get-Content implementation/flows/src/re_frame/flows/topo.cljc`

title: audit(performance): implementation/schemas
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

- `implementation/schemas` is the optional schema attachment and validation surface for re-frame2.
- Its steady-state runtime work is mostly dev-only: validation around events, coeffects, effects, subscription returns, and post-commit `app-db`.
- Its smaller always-on/runtime-adjacent surface is registration/query, boundary validation in production when `validate-at-boundary` is used, and schema-digest reads for SSR, epoch, story, and pair/tooling flows.
- Bundle cost is already explicitly tracked: `implementation/scripts/check-schemas-bundle.cjs` documents roughly `97.2 KB` gzipped for `re-frame.schemas` without Malli and `120.8 KB` with Malli.

## Likely hot paths

- `implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc` `validate-app-db!`: runs after every committing event in dev and walks every registered `app-db` schema for the frame.
- `implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/validate.cljc` `validate-event!`, `validate-cofx!`, `validate-fx!`, `validate-sub-return!`: dev-time per-dispatch/per-recompute hooks.
- `implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/digest.cljc` `app-schemas-digest`: full digest recomputation on every call.
- `implementation/schemas/src/re_frame/schemas/walker.cljc`: whole-schema flag/sensitivity walks on failure paths and elision population.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- The dev/prod split is well-designed. The `validate-*` entry points are gated at the outermost `interop/debug-enabled?` layer, and the slice has dedicated prod-mode tests/probes for DCE behavior.
- Production still pays for boundary validation when apps opt into `re-frame.spec/validate-at-boundary`, and for digest reads used by SSR/epoch/story.
- The main production cost is dependency reachability, not validator execution. Malli remains opt-in through `re-frame.schemas.malli`.

## Findings

1. `validate-app-db!` is the dominant dev-time cost center. It is `O(number of registered app-db schemas + validator cost)` after every commit, even when a dispatch changed a small subtree.
2. `app-schemas-digest` is uncached and recomputes from scratch on every read: rebuild schema map, canonical-print each schema, hash each entry, sort lines, hash again. That is fine for rare hydrate/restore paths, but it is unnecessary repeated work for story/pair/tooling surfaces.
3. Static schema-derived data is recomputed in multiple places: digest printing/hashing, sensitive-path extraction, and large/sensitive declaration aggregation. This is mostly not success-path work, but it is duplicated work from immutable inputs.
4. No obvious uncommented hot paths were found. The important runtime-sensitive paths already explain their cost model and dev/prod behavior.

## Recommended changes

- Highest value: add a per-frame digest cache invalidated by `reg-app-schema`, `restore-schemas-by-frame!`, and `clear-schemas-by-frame!`. This removes repeated full digest recomputation without changing public behavior.
- Next only if profiling shows real pain: precompute immutable schema derivatives at registration time, such as canonical printed schema text/hash and extracted `:large?` / `:sensitive?` declarations, then reuse them from stored schema metadata.
- Do not add incremental dirty-path `app-db` validation unless real workloads justify it. The upside could be large, but the implementation complexity would spill outside this slice.
- Preserve the current comment density if any optimization lands here. The existing hot-path notes are useful and already doing the right job.

## Spec impact

None

title: audit(performance): implementation/routing
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile
- `implementation/routing` owns route registration/matching, URL synthesis, navigation events, route subscriptions, scroll strategy plumbing, nav-token stale suppression, and `:route/link`.
- Runtime split:
  - Startup/dev-heavy: `reg-route`, rank computation, regex compilation, route-table rebuilds, equal-rank shadow scans.
  - Steady-state hot paths: `match-url` on `:rf/url-changed` / `:rf.route/handle-url-change`, `route-url` on `:rf.route/navigate` and `:route/link`, `:rf/url-requested` guard checks, and `:rf.route/with-nav-token`.
- Existing optimization is good: route regexes and rank tuples are precomputed at registration time, and the route table is cached in rank order.

## Likely hot paths
- `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing.cljc:422-506` `match-url`. Commented as perf-sensitive.
- `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing.cljc:532-663` `route-url`. Not performance-commented.
- `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing.cljc:804-896`, `1038-1152`, `1154-1234` navigation handlers. Behavior-commented, not cost-commented.
- `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing.cljc:1476-1533` `route-link-render` / SSR render. Render-path and not performance-commented.
- `implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing.cljc:209-272` route-table rebuild path. Commented and mostly dev/startup-only.

## Dev vs prod considerations
- Dev/hot-reload pays the heavier registration costs: route-table rebuilds and equal-rank scans in `reg-route`.
- Prod navigation still has worst-case `O(route-count)` matching, but the current cache avoids the much worse per-navigation sort/reparse path.
- Browser clients additionally pay `route-link` render and DOM-scroll costs; SSR/server traffic mainly pays `match-url` plus URL-driven slice writes.

## Findings
1. `match-url` eagerly parses and decodes the query string before any route matches (`routing.cljc:450-460`). That allocation/decoding work happens on every URL-driven navigation, including unmatched URLs and routes that never use query params.
2. Query coercion repeatedly walks the Malli `:query` vector per key (`routing.cljc:354-382`, used at `471-476`). For matched URLs this is `O(query-keys x query-schema-width)`. This is a real hot-path cost and it is not called out as such in comments.
3. `route-url` reparses the route pattern and revalidates params/query on every call (`routing.cljc:532-663`). That is fine for occasional programmatic navigation, but it also sits on the render path through `route-link-render` / `route-link-render-ssr` (`routing.cljc:1503-1533`). If large link lists rerender often, this becomes noticeable. `route-url` and `route-link-render` should have hot-path comments if left as-is.
4. Scroll restore lookup is wired, but scroll capture is not. `save-scroll-position` is only referenced by tests, not by runtime code, while `:restore` lookups exist in the navigation handlers. Performance impact today is low because the write path is effectively dead, but future wiring should avoid extra db churn on fragment-only or suppressed-scroll navigations.
5. The route-table cache invalidation check is cheap. `registrar/handlers` returns the stored map directly (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/registrar.cljc:221-226`), so the identity check in `route-table` is not itself a concern.

## Recommended changes
- Defer query parsing/coercion until after the first path match is found. Path matching does not depend on query params, so this should cut hot-path allocations with low implementation risk.
- Precompute per-route query coercion metadata at `reg-route` time, similar to the existing rank/compiled-regex precompute. A simple `{query-key -> type/coercer}` map is enough.
- Do not add a trie or more complex route index yet. The current `O(route-count)` scan is probably fine unless route counts get large and profiling shows `match-url` dominating.
- If profiling shows `route-link` rendering is hot, precompile URL-emission metadata for `route-url` at registration time. If not, at least add comments noting that `route-url` and `route-link-render` are render-path code.
- When scroll capture is wired, write saved positions only on full navigations where restore is meaningful; avoid extra writes on fragment-only changes.

## Spec impact
None

## Commands checked
- `bd prime`
- `rg --files implementation/routing`
- `Get-ChildItem -Force implementation\\routing`
- `Get-Content implementation\\routing\\src\\re_frame\\routing.cljc`
- `Get-Content implementation\\routing\\test\\re_frame\\routing_test.clj`
- `Get-Content implementation\\routing\\test\\re_frame\\route_link_test.clj`
- `Get-Content implementation\\routing\\test\\re_frame\\route_link_cljs_test.cljs`
- `Get-Content implementation\\routing\\test\\re_frame\\late_bind_missing_test.clj`

- `rg -n "save-scroll-position|rf.route/scroll-positions|..." implementation`

title: audit(performance): implementation/machines
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

`implementation/machines` is the state-machine runtime: a pure transition engine (`transition.cljc`, `parallel.cljc`, `path_walk.cljc`, `result.cljc`) plus lifecycle/timer fx handlers (`lifecycle_fx/*`, `timer.cljc`). The steady-state hot path is per-machine event handling. Secondary hot paths appear when apps lean on actor spawning, `:invoke-all`, or many live `:after` timers.

## Likely hot paths

- `re-frame.machines.transition/machine-transition-single`: event pick, exit/action/entry cascade, `:raise` drain, `:always` loop, tag recompute.
- `re-frame.machines.parallel/parallel-machine-transition` and `apply-initial-entry-cascade`: broadcast across active regions, shared-`data` threading, fx prefixing, tag union recompute.
- `re-frame.machines.path-walk/walk-path-leaf-to-root`: used by normal transition pick, `:after` pick, `:always` pick, and `:invoke-all` interception.
- `re-frame.machines.timer/after-schedule-fx`, `on-sub-changed!`, and `after-cancel-fx`: timer install/reschedule/cancel under `:after`.
- `re-frame.machines.lifecycle-fx.spawn/spawn-fx`, `destroy-machine-fx`, `finalize-machine`, and join interception for actor-heavy workloads.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Trace density is high throughout this slice. A cross-check of `implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc` shows trace emission is intended to elide in production via `debug-enabled?`, so this is mainly a dev/test cost unless prod tracing is deliberately left on.
- SSR/server mode avoids real wall-clock timer scheduling; `:after` still flows through the pure transition layer but timer installation is skipped.
- Registration-time validation is mostly a dev concern for normal top-level machine registration, but it becomes a prod concern in this slice because spawned actors currently go back through `reg-machine*`.

## Findings

- `spawn-fx` re-enters full registration work for every spawned actor. For `:machine-id` spawns, it resolves an already-registered spec and then calls `reg-machine*`, which re-runs `create-machine-handler` and `validate-machine!` over the whole spec tree before installing the live handler. In actor-heavy flows, spawn cost scales with machine-definition size instead of just instance setup cost. This is the clearest avoidable prod hot spot. The lifecycle is documented, but the performance sensitivity of this path is not; if it stays, add a comment.
- `walk-path-leaf-to-root` is on a genuine hot path and currently re-descends from the root for every prefix via `node-at*`. That makes deepest-wins lookup effectively O(depth^2) per picker call. Because the same helper backs normal event dispatch, `:after`, `:always`, and `:invoke-all` join interception, deep hierarchical machines multiply that cost quickly.
- Parallel-region fx accumulation does avoidable copying. Both `apply-initial-entry-cascade` and `parallel-machine-transition` build `acc-fx` with `vec (concat acc-fx prefixed-fx))` on each region step, which turns fx accumulation into repeated full-vector copying when several regions emit work.
- `after-cancel-fx` is still O(timers-in-frame) for each cancel because it scans the frame's whole timer table and filters by `:parent` + `:invoke`. The current design is probably fine for small timer populations and is already commented well, but timer-heavy apps or tests with many concurrent actors could feel this.

## Recommended changes

- Add a fast spawn path for registered machine templates. For `:machine-id` spawns, reuse cached validated/compiled registration data instead of routing back through `reg-machine*`. Keep full validation for inline `:definition` spawns.
- Replace region-loop `vec (concat ...)` accumulation with `into` or a transient-backed vector in `parallel.cljc`. This is low complexity and directly targets a per-event path.
- If real workloads use deep state hierarchies, refactor deepest-wins walking to traverse the active path once and reuse resolved `[prefix node]` pairs across pickers. If you keep the current structure, add a comment stating that the O(depth^2) walk is an accepted tradeoff.
- Only add a secondary timer index if profiling shows many concurrent `:after` timers per frame. The benefit could be real, but the data-structure complexity is not justified by this audit alone.

## Spec impact

None

## Commands checked

- `bd prime`
- `git status --short`
- `rg --files implementation/machines`
- `rg -n "^\\((ns|defn|defn-|defmulti|defmethod|def )" implementation/machines/src/re_frame ...`
- `rg -n "walk-path-leaf-to-root|spawn-fx|validate-machine!|after-cancel-fx|vec \\(concat|..." implementation/machines/src/re_frame ...`
- `Get-Content` with line-numbered inspection for the source files listed below
- `rg -n "defn emit!|defn emit-error!|debug-enabled?" implementation/core/...`
- `Get-Content implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc`

No benchmark or test command was run; this was a static audit.

- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines.cljc`

title: audit(performance): implementation/adapters
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

- `implementation/adapters/reagent`, `uix`, and `helix` are mostly thin substrate wiring. Reagent mostly delegates steady-state cost to Reagent itself; UIx and Helix mostly delegate it to the shared React-hook spine.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim` is the main slice-local runtime surface. It owns reactive primitives, component wrapping, hiccup-to-React conversion, batching, React 19 mount/hydrate, and static-markup serialization.
- In steady state, the real work is concentrated in `reagent-slim` render/reactivity code and in the shared UIx/Helix `use-subscribe` path.

## Likely hot paths

- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/template.cljs`: `as-element`, `vec-to-elem`, `make-element`, `convert-props`, `convert-prop-value`, `expand-seq`.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/component.cljs`: `wrap-render`, `make-render-method`, `fn-to-class`.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/ratom.cljs`: `deref-capture`, `Reaction._update-watching`, `Reaction._run`, `flush!`.
- `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/batching.cljs`: `queue-render!`, `flush-render`, `flush!`.
- UIx/Helix adapter behavior depends on `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:469-490` (`use-subscribe` via `useSyncExternalStore`).
- Major hot paths are already commented, except for the function-prop branch in `convert-prop-value`, where the code and docstring disagree.

## Dev vs prod considerations

- Source-coord stamping and related warn-once paths are correctly treated as dev-only and have prod-elision coverage in Reagent, UIx, and Helix prod tests.
- `reagent2.dom.client/flush-views!` is debug/test-only and should not influence prod tuning.
- `warn-once-keyword-prop!` is debug-only.
- `reagent2.dom.server` only matters for SSR/static export users; its cost is irrelevant for client-only apps.

## Findings

1. UIx/Helix `use-subscribe` is on a hot path and currently memoizes on raw `query-v` identity in React deps (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:469-490`). Fresh CLJS query vectors can therefore force a cache-hit `subs/subscribe` call on every render. The cleanup path removes only the watch, not a paired `subs/unsubscribe`, even though the surrounding comment says unmount should decrement the sub-cache ref-count (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs:392-404`). This is at least extra per-render churn in both dev and prod, and the code/comment mismatch should be resolved.
2. `reagent-slim` wraps every function prop in a fresh variadic closure (`implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/template.cljs:244-257`). That work sits under `convert-props` and `native-element`, so it runs on normal render paths (`implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/template.cljs:309-321`, `485-500`, `563-573`). It also defeats referential stability for handlers/refs even when the caller passed a stable function. The docstring says functions "pass through", so this hot branch currently lacks a trustworthy rationale.
3. No major slice-local issue stood out in the classic Reagent adapter or in the thin UIx/Helix adapter namespaces themselves. Their expensive behavior is delegated elsewhere. The meaningful slice-local runtime surface is `reagent-slim`.

## Recommended changes

- In the shared React spine used by UIx/Helix, stop keying `use-subscribe` resubscription work on raw CLJS vector identity. Use a stable value-equality key or a ref-based compare, and make the cleanup path explicitly symmetric with the subscription-cache contract if that is still the intended model.
- In `reagent-slim` `convert-prop-value`, benchmark direct pass-through for plain CLJS fns. If some non-JS-callable `IFn` cases still require wrapping, narrow the wrapper to those cases only and document why.
- Leave `wrap-render`, `Reaction`, and batching largely alone unless profiling shows otherwise. They are hot, but they already contain targeted optimizations and good explanatory comments.
- Add or correct a hot-path comment around the function-prop branch in `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/src/reagent2/impl/template.cljs`; most other hot paths are already commented well enough.

title: audit(performance): implementation/core
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile
`implementation/core` is the runtime kernel: frame lifecycle, per-frame routing/drain, interceptor execution, subscriptions and sub-cache, fx/cofx dispatch, trace/elision, adapter delegation, and CLJS view wrapping. In steady-state prod, the hottest paths are `dispatch` -> router drain -> interceptor chain -> `:db` commit / flows / `:fx`, plus cache-hit `subscribe` and any always-on `event-emit` / `error-emit` listeners. In dev, trace emission, render tracing, ring-buffer writes, and warn-once checks add noticeable overhead.

## Likely hot paths
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc`: `build-envelope`, `prepare-handler-ctx`, `run-chain`, `commit-and-flow!`, `drain-loop!`, `dispatch!`, `dispatch-sync!`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/subs.cljc`: `subscribe`, `validate-and-trace`, `make-layer-1-memoised-body`, `make-layer-n-memoised-body`, `unsubscribe`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/fx.cljc`: `handle-one-fx`, `do-fx`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/elision.cljc`: `elide-wire-value` / `walk`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/event_emit.cljc`, `error_emit.cljc`, `trace.cljc`: listener fan-out and envelope construction
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views.cljs`: registered view render wrapper

## Dev vs prod considerations
- Dev/prod separation is mostly strong. `trace`, source-coord annotation, render warnings, and call-site stamping sit behind `interop/debug-enabled?`, and perf marks are default-off behind `re-frame.performance/enabled?`.
- The main prod latency surface is the always-on event/error emit path. It is cheap when no listeners are registered, but once listeners exist, payload size and listener work are on the steady-state path.
- `dispatch-sync!`, trace-buffer filtering, and most warn-once logic are mainly dev/test/SSR surfaces, so extra complexity there needs a higher bar than changes on the ordinary `dispatch` path.

## Findings
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/elision.cljc` re-resolves the frame elision registry on every recursive `walk` step. Deep payloads therefore pay repeated frame lookup + app-db read even though the registry is constant for the whole call. This is a real prod hot path whenever `event-emit` / `error-emit` listeners are installed. The code comments mention avoiding repeated `assoc` on `opts`, but not this cost; if it stays as-is, that should be commented.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc` allocates fresh override maps and a fresh interceptor vector for every handled event, even on the common path with no extra frame interceptors and no overrides. This sits directly inside the steady-state dispatch path in both dev and prod.
- The always-on observability path is intentionally synchronous: router -> `event_emit/dispatch-on-event!` does a registrar lookup, elision walk, and listener fan-out before returning. That is correct by contract, but it means prod latency scales directly with listener count and event payload size. This hot-path cost is only partly obvious from the current comments.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/subs.cljc` already contains a worthwhile optimization on the hottest sub path: the layer-1 fixed-arity memo wrapper avoids per-recompute varargs/seq work. The dedicated tests around it are good and this specialization is worth keeping.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc` remains intentionally expensive in dev because delivery is synchronous and linear in emitted events and listener count, but the compile-time gates are good enough that I would not add more complexity here without measurement.

## Recommended changes
- Thread the elision registry through `elide-wire-value` once per top-level call instead of re-reading it at every recursive node. This is the clearest high-value change in the slice.
- Add a common-case fast path in `router/apply-overrides` and `router/prepare-handler-ctx`: when there are no per-frame/per-call overrides and no extra frame interceptors, reuse the handler interceptor vector and shared empty maps instead of building new ones.
- Treat `event-emit` / `error-emit` listeners as budgeted production features: keep listener bodies minimal, move shipping/network work out of the synchronous callback where possible, and avoid large event vectors.
- Add short hot-path comments where the current cost is intentional but not obvious, especially in `elision/walk` and the router interceptor/override assembly path.
- Do not spend effort further optimizing dev-only trace/buffer machinery unless profiling shows it matters.

## Spec impact
None

## Commands checked
- `bd prime`

- `Get-ChildItem implementation/core/src/re_frame -Recurse -File | ... Measure-Object -Line`

title: audit(performance): implementation/epoch
description:
# Slice Performance Audit

## Current purpose / runtime profile

`implementation/epoch` is the optional dev/pair-tool epoch layer: it captures per-frame trace events, assembles `:rf/epoch-record` values at drain-settle, stores a bounded per-frame history, fans records out to epoch listeners, and exposes `restore-epoch` / `reset-frame-db!`.

The runtime cost is concentrated in dev-style execution: per-trace capture on every emitted trace event, then per-drain record assembly. `restore-epoch`, `reset-frame-db!`, and frame-destroy cleanup are real code paths but not steady-state hot paths.

## Likely hot paths

- `capture-event!` and `buffer-event!` (`implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:397`, `:353`) run for every trace event once the epoch artefact is loaded.
- `settle!` and `build-record` (`implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:594`, `:571`) run once per drain and re-walk the captured event vector several times.
- `record!`, `append-record`, and `elide-older-trace-events` (`implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:149`, `:141`, `:123`) are hot when history is enabled, especially if `:trace-events-keep` is set.
- `notify-listeners!` / `record-observation!` (`implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:267`, `:237`) are per-drain x per-listener; the steady-state no-op guard is already present and tested.

## Dev vs prod considerations

CLJS production looks clean: the slice bodies are gated on `interop/debug-enabled?`, and CLJS binds that to `goog.DEBUG` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.cljs:152`). In `:advanced` production builds, the epoch machinery should DCE away.

JVM/CLJ is different: `interop/debug-enabled?` is always `true` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.clj:105`), so tests and tool/server-side hosts always pay epoch costs once this artefact is loaded. Also, loading the artefact expands core trace delivery through the late-bound epoch capture hook on every emit (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc:334`).

## Findings

1. `:trace-events-keep` currently makes append cost scale with retained history size. `append-record` always routes through `elide-older-trace-events`, which rewrites the whole retained vector with `map-indexed`/`dissoc` when the knob is set (`implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:123-147`). This is the clearest avoidable hot-path cost in the slice.
2. Record assembly is multipass. Each settle does separate walks for trigger extraction, `:sub-runs`, `:renders`, and `:effects` (`implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:523-590`). That is acceptable for moderate cascades, but it is the dominant per-drain CPU cost for large dev/JVM workloads.
3. The steady-state per-trace capture path is intentionally small, but it still pays one atom `swap!` per trace event (`implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc:353-354`). That looks like the feature's baseline cost rather than an accidental inefficiency.
4. Hot-path commentary is strong around `capture-event!`, `find-trigger-event`, and `record-observation!`, but thinner around `buffer-event!` and the `append-record` / `elide-older-trace-events` path. Those should get short perf-oriented comments before further tuning work lands there.

## Recommended changes

- Optimize `:trace-events-keep` maintenance first. Avoid reprocessing the whole retained history on every append; only the newly out-of-window record and the new tail record need attention.
- Keep the current multipass settle code unless profiling shows large-cascade latency. If it does, fuse trigger detection plus the three projections into one reducer; that is the only complexity increase here with likely meaningful payoff.
- Add short hot-path comments to `buffer-event!` and `append-record` explaining expected frequency and complexity, since those are the least self-explanatory performance-sensitive paths.
- Treat this artefact as opt-in for dev workflows. If a tool or app does not need epochs/time-travel, not loading `re-frame.epoch` avoids adding this slice to the trace hot path at all.

## Spec impact

None

## Commands checked

- `bd prime`
- `Get-ChildItem -Force implementation\\epoch`
- `rg --files implementation/epoch`
- `rg -n "epoch|hot path|perf|performance|debug|assert|trace|log|warn" implementation/epoch`
- `rg -n "debug-enabled\\?|epoch/capture-event|epoch/settle!|trace-events-keep|register-epoch-cb!|restore-epoch|reset-frame-db!" .`
- `Get-Content` slices for the implementation and neighboring runtime files listed below

## Files checked

- `implementation/epoch/deps.edn`
- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc`
- `implementation/epoch/test/re_frame/epoch_test.clj`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/trace.cljc`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/core_epoch.cljc`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/router.cljc`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.cljs`
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/interop.clj`
