title: Server error sanitisation boundary — public projection of SSR errors
description:
React Router explicitly sanitises server errors before they reach the browser in production. The current re-frame2 spec has structured errors and mismatch tracing (009), but does NOT clearly separate:

- Internal/server diagnostic detail (stack traces, exception data, internal codes) → trace surface only.
- Public/client-safe error detail → response payload.

Without this boundary, SSR error pages can leak stack traces, secrets in exception messages, and internal codes to clients.

## Concrete benefit

- No stack traces or secrets leaked to the client.
- Predictable 404/401/500 output.
- Cleaner monitoring and error reporting (full detail in traces; sanitised in response).
- A stable public error shape that SSR fallback templates can rely on.

## Fit with re-frame2

The right move is **not** to invent React-style error boundaries in the SSR core. It's to define a **public projection** of server errors that sits between the structured trace event (rich, internal) and the client-bound response (clean, public).

This fits 009's structured-error direction naturally: the internal :rf.error/* event is preserved in the trace; a sanitisation step produces the public projection for the response.

## Mechanism

Keep the full internal error trace event (per 009). Add a public error shape:

  {:status     500
   :code       :internal-error
   :message    "Something went wrong"
   :retryable? false}

Mapping rule:

1. SSR rendering / setup errors emit the full structured trace event (existing).
2. Before serialising anything to the client (or rendering an error page), the runtime maps the internal error to a public error shape via a registered projector.
3. Known control-flow errors preserve more detail:
   - :404 not found
   - :redirect
   - :validation-failure
   - :unauthorised
4. Unknown exceptions become a generic 500 in production by default. In dev, the public shape can include more detail (configurable via :ssr config).

## Customisation

Two plausible mechanisms:

1. **Registered projector.** (rf/reg-error-projector :myapp/public-error (fn [trace-event] public-shape)). Single registered projector consulted on each server error.
2. **Config-driven.** (rf/configure :ssr {:public-error-id :myapp/public-error}) names the projector to use.

**Lean: both.** A reg-* fn for the projector itself; a configure call to declare which one is active. Allows per-host customisation while keeping the registry-first pattern.

## Default projector

re-frame2 ships a default projector that:
- Maps known categories (:rf.error/no-such-handler → 404 in routing context, etc.).
- Generic 500 with code :internal-error and message "Something went wrong" for unknowns.
- In dev mode (configurable), includes :details with the original trace event.

Users who want different rules register their own projector and configure :ssr to use it.

## Open design calls

1. **Where in the pipeline does sanitisation happen?** Before HTML response render (inside the SSR pipeline) or at the host-adapter boundary (in the wrapper code)? Lean: before render. The HTML response IS the public projection; rendering an error page reads the public shape.

2. **Dev vs prod default behaviour.** Dev shows full detail; prod shows generic. Configurable via :ssr config or by the projector itself reading a build-time flag.

3. **Mapping for known errors.** :rf.error/no-such-handler in routing context → 404. :rf.error/schema-validation-failure → 400. Document the canonical mapping in the default projector.

4. **What about errors from within views (render-time)?** View exceptions during SSR also need projection. Same mechanism applies; document.

## Files to update when actioning

- 011-SSR.md: new §Server error projection; document the public error shape; document the projector mechanism; document the default projector; document dev vs prod behaviour.
- 009-Instrumentation.md: cross-reference the public-projection step from the structured-error contract; clarify that internal trace events are not leaked to the client.
- Spec-Schemas.md: add :rf/public-error schema; document the trace-event → public-error projection contract.
- API.md: add reg-error-projector row; add :ssr config keys for projector configuration; add :rf.error/sanitised-on-projection trace event for cases where the runtime had to fall back to the generic error.
- 001-Registration.md: add :error-projector registry kind.
- conformance/fixtures/: 2 fixtures: ssr-error-sanitisation.edn (handler throws; verify response contains generic 500 with no stack trace; verify trace contains full detail), ssr-error-known-mapping.edn (routing 404; verify response is 404 status with appropriate public shape).

## Why P2 (not P1)

Security/operational hygiene. Apps without it 'work' but leak diagnostic detail. P2 because:
- The trace surface already exists; this is a new use of existing data.
- Default projector covers most cases; users only register custom ones for specialised needs.
- Production-mode default is the safe default (generic 500); the worst-case behaviour without this bead is information leakage, not broken pages.

## Pairs with

- 009-Instrumentation.md structured error contract (the source of internal trace events).
- rf2-aspv (P1 HTTP response contract) — public error projection populates :status / :headers in the response.
- rf2-5pt (AI implementability) — closes a security best-practice gap that production SSR needs.

Status: open. Design proposed; four open calls flagged. Estimated effort: medium focused agent pass.
close_reason: Specced server error sanitisation boundary: :rf/public-error shape, reg-error-projector registry kind, default projector with canonical mapping, before-render placement, dev/prod gating, view-time exception handling, sanitised-on-projection fallback, two conformance fixtures.

title: First-class head/meta contract for SSR — derived-from-state head model
description:
The current 011-SSR.md spec is strong on body rendering but says nothing substantive about head metadata (title, meta tags, canonical URLs, Open Graph, Twitter cards, structured data, etc.). All admired SSR frameworks (Next.js, Nuxt, React Router) make this a first-class concern.

For SSR specifically, head tags belong in the server-rendered HTML (so crawlers see them on first byte), not as a later browser mutation. This is the central reason head/meta needs SSR-level treatment.

## Concrete benefit

- Correct initial <title> and meta tags.
- Canonical URLs for SEO.
- Robots directives.
- Open Graph / Twitter cards (link-unfurling on social platforms).
- Structured data (JSON-LD).
- Tooling can inspect the head model without scraping templates.

## Fit with re-frame2

Fits cleanly **only if treated as data produced from state**, not as an imperative DOM API.

Bad fit (don't do):
- Mutate the document head from inside components ('useHead'-style imperative API).

Good fit (do):
- A pure head model derived from app-db, route, and props.
- Computed during render; serialised as HTML head; client recomputes/confirms on hydration.

Preserves testability, portability, AI-amenability.

## Mechanism

Standard head model:

  {:title "Article title"
   :meta  [{:name "description" :content "..."}
           {:property "og:title" :content "..."}]
   :link  [{:rel "canonical" :href "https://example.com/articles/123"}]
   :html-attrs {}
   :body-attrs {}}

Three plausible exposure surfaces (pick one):

1. **Route metadata** — :head on a route is a pure function or sub-id deriving the head from app-db + route + params.
2. **Registered head function** — (rf/reg-head id ?metadata f) where f is pure like a view; (rf/render-head head-id) emits the head map.
3. **Pure helper over root view** — (rf/render-head frame-id root-view-id props).

**Lean: registered head function** + route :head metadata that names which registered head to use. Keeps head policy enumerable through (handlers :head); separates head/SEO logic from body rendering; pure and testable.

## Default flow

1. SSR request renders the body view.
2. Runtime resolves the active route's :head metadata to a registered head id.
3. (rf/render-head head-id frame-id) returns the head model.
4. Server emits <head>...</head> from the model.
5. Client on hydration recomputes the head from current state (no DOM scraping).
6. Mismatch detection: client compares its computed head to the rendered head; emits :rf.warning/head-mismatch if different.

Optional: tooling exposes (rf/active-head) to query the current head model without re-rendering.

## Open design calls

1. **Default head when no route declares :head.** Sensible default: title from frame metadata, content-type meta, charset meta. Or strict: registration must declare a head; missing emits :rf.error/no-head-registered.

2. **Composition across routes.** Should nested routes compose head fragments (parent + child)? Or is it always a single :head per route? Lean: single :head per route to start; composition is a follow-up if real cases emerge.

3. **Head mismatch handling.** Same as body-render mismatch: detect and warn; client re-renders to its computed head. Or: server head wins (don't override on hydration). Lean: detect-and-warn but client re-renders (consistency with body-mismatch handling).

4. **JSON-LD / structured data shape.** A flat :scripts vector? Or a dedicated :json-ld field? Lean: include in :script or a dedicated :json-ld field for clarity.

## Files to update when actioning

- 011-SSR.md: new §Head/meta contract; document the head model shape; document the registered-head mechanism; document hydration recomputation; document mismatch detection.
- Spec-Schemas.md: add :rf/head-model schema (title, meta, link, html-attrs, body-attrs, scripts, json-ld).
- API.md: add reg-head row; add render-head row; add :rf.warning/head-mismatch warning category.
- 001-Registration.md: add :head registry kind to the per-kind list; document the metadata shape for registered heads.
- conformance/fixtures/: 2 fixtures: ssr-head-emits.edn (verify <title> and meta tags appear in rendered HTML), ssr-head-hydration.edn (verify client-computed head matches server-rendered head).

## Why P2 (not P1)

Important but not correctness-blocking. Apps without explicit head support work; they just don't render correct SEO/social metadata server-side. Worth shipping a standard answer for production use.

## Pairs with

- 011 existing render-to-string story (head rendering is a sibling concern).
- 012 routing — :head is a route-metadata key.
- rf2-5pt (AI implementability) — closes a real-world feature most apps need.
- rf2-aspv (P1 HTTP response contract) — head-tags include status-aware bits like canonical URLs that may depend on the response status.

Status: open. Design proposed; four open calls flagged. Estimated effort: medium focused agent pass.
close_reason: Specced derived-from-state head/meta contract: :rf/head-model schema, reg-head registry kind, route :head metadata pointer, render-head/active-head, single-head-per-route in v1, head-mismatch detection, two conformance fixtures.

title: re-frame2 ships pair-required infra in-tree — eliminate re-frame-pair's dependency on re-frame-10x
description:
Today re-frame-pair (the nREPL-attached AI/REPL companion) requires re-frame-10x to be installed in the host application. The dependency exists because pair leans on infrastructure that historically lives in 10x — trace buffering, epoch history per drain-completion, source-coord query, frame-snapshot introspection.

re-frame2 should ship that infrastructure in-tree as part of the framework's standard surface, so that:

1. **re-frame-pair becomes a thin REPL/nREPL consumer of re-frame2's standard tooling primitives** — no 10x dependency required.
2. **A new re-frame-10x can be rewritten as a thin UI on top of re-frame2's standard tooling primitives** — sharing the substrate with pair instead of providing its own.
3. **Future AI tools (pair-improver per rf2-ps4, custom debug panels, story tools per 007) consume the same standard surface.**

The principle: re-frame2 owns the *infrastructure* (data shapes, query APIs, retention policies); 10x and pair own the *presentation/orchestration* on top.

## What infra moves in-tree

Most of the surface is already specified in Tool-Pair.md and 009-Instrumentation.md as v1-required. This bead is to verify the surface is *complete* and *integrated* enough that an external consumer like re-frame-pair (with no 10x dependency) can do its job.

Specific surface re-frame-pair needs:

1. **Trace buffer.** Last N trace events retained in-runtime, queryable. Today 10x keeps this; should be a runtime primitive in re-frame2 (in-tree, dev-only, configurable depth).
2. **Epoch history.** Per-frame snapshots at drain-completion boundaries. Specced in Tool-Pair §Epoch history; verify the implementation surface is complete.
3. **Source-coord query.** `(handler-meta :event :foo)` returns `{:ns :line :file :doc :source?}`. Already specced; verify surface.
4. **Public registrar query API.** `(handlers :event)`, `(machines)`, `(machine-meta)`. Already specced.
5. **Frame metadata introspection.** `(frame-ids)`, `(frame-meta frame-id)`. Already specced.
6. **Snapshot snapshot.** `(snapshot-of frame-id)` or `(get-frame-db frame-id)`. Already specced.
7. **Sub-cache introspection.** `(sub-cache frame-id)` for understanding what's currently subscribed. Already specced (CLJS-only).
8. **Hot-swap interface.** Re-register handlers at runtime; pair uses this for AI-driven exploration. Already specced via standard reg-* API.
9. **fx-stub mechanism.** Per-call override of fx for tests/AI experimentation. Already specced via `:fx-overrides` in dispatch opts.

## What needs verification (action items)

1. **Audit Tool-Pair.md against current spec.** Is every item Tool-Pair claims as v1-required actually specified in the per-feature specs? Cross-check.
2. **Audit re-frame-pair's actual usage of 10x.** Identify every place pair imports from 10x's namespaces; verify each has a re-frame2 in-tree equivalent.
3. **Trace buffer:** confirm the spec mandates a built-in trace buffer in dev builds. 009 §Subscription/consumption documents register-trace-cb / remove-trace-cb but doesn't explicitly require a built-in retain-N-events buffer. Add this if missing.
4. **Epoch history config:** verify `(rf/configure :epoch-history {:depth N})` is in API.md and is the canonical configuration surface for pair-style consumers.
5. **Production elision:** confirm the entire pair-required surface is dev-only — no production-build cost. Tool-Pair already states this; verify.
6. **Document the consumption pattern.** A short §'How AI tools attach' note in Tool-Pair.md or a new Companion doc that says: 'consumers register as trace listeners + query the registrar + read epoch history; that's the entire surface; no 10x dependency required.'

## Knock-on for re-frame-10x

When this lands, re-frame-10x v2 can be rewritten as:
- A registered trace listener.
- A renderer of the in-tree epoch history.
- A query consumer of the registrar.
- A UI on top — *not* a dependency.

That decouples 10x from pair entirely. They can share the substrate without one depending on the other.

## Pairs with

- Tool-Pair.md (the spec for pair-shaped tools — defines the contract).
- 009-Instrumentation.md (trace surface — needs to host the trace buffer in-tree).
- rf2-ps4 (re-frame-pair-improver skill, deferred — same family of tooling).
- rf2-13lo (Implementor Checklist — the pair-required surface should be in the Tool-Pair section of the Part 2 checklist).
- rf2-edi (006 revertibility audit — adapter shouldn't hold tool-relevant state outside the frame value, otherwise pair sees inconsistent state).

## Why P2

Real product impact: re-frame-pair's current 10x dependency is a friction point for users who want pair-style AI assistance without a 10x panel. Making re-frame2 self-sufficient for pair-shape tools removes the friction and enables the multi-impl story (re-frame-js, re-frame-py would each ship their own pair-required surface, not depend on a 10x-equivalent existing).

Action when the spec is closer to lock and the per-feature specs (009, Tool-Pair) have stabilised. Until then, this bead serves as the consolidating reminder that pair-required infra is a *framework concern*, not a 10x concern.

Status: open. P2 — affects the multi-impl story and the pair tooling experience.
close_reason: Audited pair-required surface against current spec. 8 of 9 items already specified (epoch history, source coords, registrar query API, frame metadata, snapshot-of, sub-cache, hot-swap, fx-stub). Gap: 009 explicitly disclaimed a long-term trace buffer ('tools maintain their own'). Added normative §Retain-N trace ring buffer (dev-only) to 009 specifying (rf/trace-buffer), (rf/clear-trace-buffer!), (rf/configure :trace-buffer {:depth N}); default 200 events; production-elided. Added matching API.md rows. Added §How AI tools attach to Tool-Pair.md documenting the consumption pattern: trace listener + trace buffer + epoch history + registrar query — no 10x dependency. Pair-required infra is now wholly in re-frame2's tree.

title: First-class navigation blocking — pending-nav protocol
description:
Real product need: unsaved forms, interrupted checkouts, destructive multi-step workflows. Angular, Vue Router, and TanStack Router all support blocking or confirming navigation. Current 012-Routing.md spec answer is 'use interceptors' — workable but too implicit for such a common case.

Make navigation blocking a first-class **named event/state protocol** instead of a magic component hook. This fits re-frame2 perfectly: pending-nav lives in app-db; UI renders confirm dialogs from ordinary subscriptions; user choices are dispatched normal events. All testable.

## Concrete benefit

- Real and common product need is met without re-frame2 forcing users to invent the pattern.
- Testable end-to-end via dispatched events; no special test machinery needed.
- Aligns with re-frame2 ethos: explicit state, named events, no implicit hooks.

## Mechanism

A standard pending-navigation state and three named events:

  [:route/navigation-blocked pending-nav]    ;; emitted by runtime when leave-guard rejects
  [:route/continue pending-nav-id]            ;; user dispatches to proceed
  [:route/cancel   pending-nav-id]            ;; user dispatches to abort

Route metadata can declare leave guards:

  (rf/reg-route :editor/article
    {:can-leave [:editor/can-leave?]              ;; sub-id; returns boolean
     :path "/editor/articles/:id"
     ...})

Or a frame-level policy can hook :rf/url-requested.

## Default flow

1. :rf/url-requested fires with the new URL.
2. Runtime evaluates leave guards for the *current* route (subscribes to :can-leave sub or runs a registered guard fn).
3. If clear → proceed normally (the new URL becomes active).
4. If blocked → store the intended navigation in app-db under :rf/pending-navigation; emit :route/navigation-blocked.
5. UI renders a confirmation dialog from (subscribe [:rf/pending-navigation]).
6. User chooses: dispatch [:route/continue id] or [:route/cancel id].
7. Runtime applies the choice — proceeds or stays.

## Pending-nav slot in app-db

  {:rf/pending-navigation
   {:id "pn-7"
    :requested-by-event [:rf/url-requested ...]
    :requested-url "/editor/articles/42"
    :reason "Form has unsaved changes"
    :rejecting-route :editor/article
    :rejecting-guard :editor/can-leave?}}

Cleared on :route/continue (with the navigation completing) or :route/cancel (without).

## Files to update when actioning

- 012-Routing.md: new §'Navigation blocking — pending-nav protocol'; document the three events, the slot shape, the leave-guard mechanism.
- Spec-Schemas.md: add :rf/pending-navigation schema; extend :rf/route-metadata with :can-leave field.
- conformance/fixtures/: new fixture route-navigation-blocked.edn — register a route with :can-leave; trigger nav while guard returns false; verify :rf/pending-navigation is set; verify URL did not change; dispatch :route/continue; verify URL changed.

title: Fragment support in route slice — bring #fragment into the routing contract
description:
The current 012-Routing.md spec leaves #fragment outside the routing-level contract; views are told to read window.location.hash directly. This pushes browser-ambient state back into view code, which fights the rest of the design (everything else is explicit data flowing through events).

## Concrete benefit

- Anchor navigation becomes SSR-safe and testable.
- No direct browser read needed in view code.
- Scroll behavior integrates with fragments cleanly.
- Docs pages, settings tabs, anchored sections become portable across hosts.

## Mechanism

Extend the route slice with :fragment:

  {:id       :route/docs
   :params   {:page "routing"}
   :query    {}
   :fragment "scroll-restoration"}

Extend the helpers:
- (rf/match-url url) includes :fragment in its return.
- (rf/route-url route-id path-params query-params fragment?) emits the URL with #fragment.
- :route/navigate accepts {:fragment "section-2"} in opts or in target maps.

Update :nav/scroll semantics:
- If a fragment is present and the strategy is compatible (default :top), attempt element scroll first.
- Otherwise fall back to existing strategies (:top / :restore / :preserve).

## Subtlety: fragment-only changes do NOT re-fire :on-match

Same route + same params + different fragment → the route slice updates :fragment and emits :rf/url-changed, but :on-match (the loaded-data dispatch) is NOT re-fired. Loaded data is unchanged when only the fragment changed.

Document this rule explicitly: :on-match fires when path or query changes; fragment-only changes update the slice and emit :rf/url-changed for views to react.

## Files to update when actioning

- 012-Routing.md: §Route slice — add :fragment field; §match-url / route-url — extend signatures; §:nav/scroll — fragment-aware behaviour; new §'Fragment-only navigation' callout for the :on-match exception rule.
- Spec-Schemas.md: extend :rf/route-slice with :fragment (string-or-nil).
- conformance/fixtures/: new fixture route-fragment-change.edn — navigate to URL with fragment; verify slice contains fragment; navigate to same path with different fragment; verify :on-match does NOT re-fire; verify :rf/url-changed does fire.
- 011-SSR.md: confirm SSR parses fragment from request URL when applicable (mostly relevant for static-site generators with anchored navigation).

## Why P2 (not P1)

Polish more than correctness. Nothing is broken without fragment support — views can read window.location.hash and live. But it pushes a class of state out of the deterministic, testable, explicit data flow that the rest of the spec maintains. Worth fixing.

## Pairs with

- rf2-61r0 (P1, route ranking) — fragments are matched after route resolution; ranking applies to path/query, not fragment.
- 012-Routing existing scroll-restoration spec.

Status: open. Design locked; ready to action. Estimated effort: small focused agent pass.

title: Delayed :after transitions — formalisation
description:
:after is a delayed transition — fires after a specified time delay, no event needed. xstate/SCXML term: delayed transition.

## The pattern

A state with :after declares a map of milliseconds → transition specs. Each entry runs an independent timer; on expiry, the corresponding transition fires (subject to guards). Exiting the state advances an epoch counter; in-flight timers compare epochs on receipt and ignore stale firings.

```
{:loading {:after {5000  :timeout
                   30000 :hard-error}
           :on    {:loaded :ready
                   :failed :error}}}
```

## Locked design calls

1. **Cancellation: epoch-based stale-detection.** No new fx primitive (no :cancel-dispatch-later). Each entry increments an epoch counter in the machines :data; the scheduled :dispatch-later carries the epoch at scheduling time. On receipt, machine handler compares; mismatch → silently ignored, emits :machine.timer/stale-after trace.

2. **SSR behavior: :after no-ops.** SSR mode disables timer scheduling at the entry action; in-flight timers are not created. Document the rule: :after is a client-side affordance; SSR renders the static current state without timer effects.

3. **Clock abstraction: lives in the existing re-frame.interop layer.** re-frame already has a clj/cljs-split interop layer (preserved in re-frame2 per project memory). The clock primitive is a natural addition there:

  - re-frame.interop.now-ms (host-clock current time)
  - re-frame.interop.schedule-after! (host-clock setTimeout-equivalent)
  - re-frame.interop.cancel-scheduled! (best-effort cancellation, optional)

  Tests swap the interop layer using existing test fixtures; no new clock-configuration API is needed at the framework level.

4. **Value shape: admit transition-specs and fn-valued delays.**
  - Keyword-target sugar: `{5000 :timeout}` → `{5000 {:target :timeout}}`.
  - Full transition spec: `{5000 {:guard :still-loading? :target :timeout :action :log-timeout}}`.
  - Fn-valued delays: `{(fn [snap] (* 1000 (:retry-count data))) :retry}` for parameterised timing.

5. **Trace events:** :machine.timer/scheduled, :machine.timer/fired, :machine.timer/stale-after.

6. **Hierarchy interaction:** :after on a parent state remains active while in any child. Multiple :after timers can be in flight simultaneously across hierarchy levels. Exiting a level advances that levels epoch; pending timers from that level go stale.

7. **Multiple :after per state:** all timers run independently; whichever fires first (and matches its guard) triggers its transition. The transitions exit advances the epoch; other in-flight timers go stale.

## Drain semantics interaction

:after fires through the standard event pipeline (it dispatches a future event via :dispatch-later). When the event lands, drain semantics applies normally:
  - Per Level 3, the machine handler receives the synthetic ::after-elapsed event.
  - Epoch check happens before transition lookup.
  - On match: transition fires per Level 2 ordering (exit / action / entry cascade).
  - :raise queue and :always check happen as normal after the transition.

No new microstep loop. :after is just a deferred event source.

## What :after does NOT include

- Recurring timers — :after fires once per state entry. For polling, the user re-enters the state (e.g., :fetching → :waiting → :fetching).
- Wall-clock delays — :after is relative-to-entry, not "fire at 9:00 AM tomorrow."
- Pause / resume — no built-in pause; users pause by transitioning out.

## Schema additions

:rf/state-node gains optional :after slot:
```
[:after {:optional true}
 [:map-of
  [:or pos-int? fn?]              ;; ms or (fn [snap] ms)
  [:or :keyword                    ;; sugar: target keyword
       [:map                       ;; full transition spec
        [:guard  {:optional true} :rf/guard-ref]
        [:target {:optional true} :rf/transition-target]
        [:action {:optional true} :rf/action-ref]
        [:meta   {:optional true} :map]]]]]
```

## Conformance fixtures (minimum 3)

1. after-single-delay.edn — simple delay; verify timer fires; transition occurs after configured ms.
2. after-stale-detection.edn — real event arrives first; timer fires; epoch mismatch; ignored with :machine.timer/stale-after trace.
3. after-hierarchy.edn — :after on parent state; entering child doesnt cancel; timer remains active across child transitions; exits parent → epoch advances → timer stale.

All three use the test-clock pattern (advance time deterministically via re-frame.interop test fixtures).

## Files to update when actioning

- 005-StateMachines.md: new §"Delayed :after transitions" near §Eventless :always; update §Capability matrix — flip :after from work-in-progress to specified; update §Drain semantics gotchas with new gotcha (most common: forgetting epoch increment on entry).
- 002-Frames.md (or re-frame.interop section): document the clock primitives.
- 011-SSR.md: document :after no-op rule under SSR.
- Spec-Schemas.md: add :after slot to :rf/state-node per above; new error category :rf.warning/no-clock-configured (warning, not error); new trace events.
- conformance/fixtures/: add the 3 new fixtures; ensure test-clock fixture pattern is established.
- conformance/README.md: list new fixtures.

## Pairs with

- rf2-a83 (Spec-Schemas additions for v1 WIP capabilities — :after schema closes the last piece).
- rf2-3tk (closed; hierarchical states — :after interacts with hierarchical entry/exit).
- rf2-9ln (closed; :always — sibling delayed/eventless transition; same drain interaction).

Status: open. Design is locked; ready to action via a focused agent pass like :always.

Substantive content in 005 §Delayed :after transitions.

title: State machines are an optional capability — upfront question for AI one-shot implementation
description:
An implementor (human or AI) building re-frame2 in a new language is not required to include the state-machine substrate. State machines are an optional capability the implementor declares one way or the other before starting.

Per the multi-implementation framing (rf2-vf8m): not every host needs machines. A Python or JS port targeting simple CRUD apps may legitimately ship just the foundation (events / subs / fx / interceptors / app-db / views) without machines. The pattern accommodates this — machines are a self-contained substrate that can be added later without disturbing what came before.

Action: this is one of the upfront questions an AI doing the one-shot implementation must answer first. It goes in the Implementor Checklist (rf2-13lo) under the initial-questions section.

Suggested shape for the upfront questions section of the checklist:

  Part 1 — Capability decisions (include / exclude)
    - Include state machines? (Yes / No)
    - Include routing? (Yes / No)
    - Include SSR? (Yes / No)
    - Include schemas? (Yes / No / Use host static types)
    - Include stories? (Yes / No)

  Part 2 — Per-capability detail decisions
    For each included capability, the implementor makes the per-capability choices already enumerated in rf2-13lo.

Why state machines warrant this explicit gate (where some other capabilities might be implicitly required):
  - The substrate is substantial: drain semantics extension, snapshot storage, hierarchical states, spawn/destroy, registered guards/actions, conformance fixtures. Several specs of weight.
  - The pattern works without machines — events / subs / fx / app-db / views all stand on their own.
  - Many small frameworks would ship without machines initially and add them later.
  - The conformance corpus already tags fixtures by capability, so a machine-free implementation is automatically gradable: it passes everything tagged with capabilities it claims.

Pairs with rf2-13lo (Implementor Checklist), rf2-5pt (AI can one-shot), rf2-vf8m (multi-impl org).

Status: open. P2 — feeds the Implementor Checklist when drafted. The checklist itself is in rf2-13lo; this bead captures the specific upfront-question content for the state-machines decision.
close_reason: Subsumed by rf2-13lo Part 1, which now enumerates state machines alongside routing, SSR, schemas, stories, Tool-Pair, and AI-Audit as upfront include/exclude capability decisions. The state-machines case is one of seven. Closing as redundant; rationale lives in rf2-13lo.

title: Create Implementor's Checklist — consolidated decision list for porting re-frame2 to any host
description:
An implementor (human or AI) building re-frame2 in a new language faces two sequential questions:

  1. **How complete?** — Which capabilities does this implementation include?
  2. **How achieved?** — For each included capability, what technology / library choices does it make?

A consolidated **Implementors Checklist** captures both, in that order, with options and reference-impl picks.

This is essentially a structured form of the "AI can one-shot the implementation" goal (rf2-5pt) — the checklist IS what the AI consults when porting to a new host.

---

## Part 1 — How complete? (capability decisions)

The implementor declares which optional capabilities the implementation supports. Each gates substantial chunks of the spec; declaring them upfront lets the AI scope its work.

**Required (not gated):** events, subscriptions, effects, coeffects, interceptors, app-db, frames, views, the trace surface. Every conformant implementation has these.

**Optional (declare yes/no):**

  - **State machines?** The FSM/actor substrate (Spec 005) — drain extensions, hierarchy, spawn/destroy, registered guards/actions. Substantial. Pattern works without machines (events / subs / fx / app-db / views are self-sufficient). Many small frameworks ship without machines initially.

  - **Routing?** URL ↔ frame state contract (Spec 012). Useful for SPAs; non-essential for component libraries or non-routing apps.

  - **SSR?** Server-side render + hydration (Spec 011). Useful for full-stack apps; non-essential for client-only apps.

  - **Schemas?** Boundary validation + introspection (Spec 010). Dynamic hosts (CLJS, JS, Python) likely use a schema library (Malli, Zod, Pydantic). Static hosts (TS, Rust, F#, Swift) may use the type system directly and skip a runtime schema layer (third option: "use host static types").

  - **Stories?** Stories / variants / workspaces (Spec 007). Post-v1 library territory in re-frame-cljs; an early-stage port may skip entirely.

  - **Tool-Pair adapters?** Pair-shaped AI inspection tools (Tool-Pair.md). Useful for AI-driven development; non-essential for app delivery.

  - **AI-Audit grading?** Self-grading against AI-first principles (AI-Audit.md). Useful for spec-conformance certification; non-essential at impl time.

Conformance fixtures are capability-tagged: the implementation runs whatever fixtures match its claimed capabilities; unclaimed ones are skipped. The pattern conformance bar is "passes everything you claim."

---

## Part 2 — How achieved? (technology decisions)

For each included capability (and for the always-required foundation), the implementor makes the per-capability technology/library choices below.

**Foundation (always required):**

  - Persistent data structures library (rf2-53x is the standalone bead; this checklist consolidates).
  - Reactive substrate (signals / atoms / observables).
  - Effect-handling primitive (how :fx dispatches; sync vs async).
  - Concurrency model (run-to-completion semantics).
  - Hot-reload primitive (registry replacement at runtime).

**State storage (always required):**

  - App-db container (atom / store / signal / etc.).
  - Snapshot/restore mechanism.
  - Path-access primitive (built-in or library).

**Subscriptions (always required):**

  - Signal graph + caching.
  - Lifecycle (when to dispose).

**Views (always required):**

  - Render-tree shape (hiccup / JSX / virtual-DOM nodes).
  - Render trigger.
  - Mount/unmount.

**Tracing & instrumentation (always required):**

  - Trace-event delivery (sync / async batched).
  - Performance API equivalent.
  - Production elision mechanism.

**Errors (always required):**

  - Error capture/recover.
  - Error reporting to tools.

**Testing (recommended; required for conformance):**

  - Test runner conventions.
  - Headless evaluation (compute-sub / machine-transition).
  - Conformance fixture consumption.

**Routing (if Part 1 says yes):**

  - URL primitive.
  - Navigation observer.

**SSR (if Part 1 says yes):**

  - Render-to-string.
  - Hydration boundary.
  - Platform gating.

**Schemas (if Part 1 says yes):**

  - Schema language.
  - Validation timing.
  - Introspection API.

**Machines (if Part 1 says yes):**

  - Snapshot serialisation format.
  - Spawn primitive.
  - Drain implementation.
  - Hierarchy support level.

**Tool-Pair (if Part 1 says yes):**

  - Tool-Pair adapters.

---

## Per-decision shape

Each Part-2 decision entry has:

  - Name (e.g., "Persistent data structures library").
  - Why it matters (which re-frame2 mechanic depends on this; cross-reference the goal/spec it serves).
  - Options by host (canonical choices for each major host language: JS/TS, Python, Rust, F#, Java, Swift).
  - Reference-impl picks (what re-frame-cljs uses; what re-frame-js uses per rf2-vf8m).
  - Trade-offs (criteria for choosing).

---

## Where it lives

Standalone doc — docs/specification/Implementor-Checklist.md (or similar). Per-spec sections can have small "Implementor decisions" callouts cross-referencing the canonical checklist.

Naming options: Implementor-Checklist, Host-Implementor-Guide, Implementing-re-frame, Porting-Guide. Lean: Implementor-Checklist (terse, matches the artefacts purpose).

---

## Pairs with

  - rf2-5pt (AI can one-shot the implementation) — the checklist is the structured form of this goal.
  - rf2-53x (PDS dependency, which this consolidates).
  - rf2-vf8m (multi-impl org).
  - rf2-edi (006 revertibility audit, which informs adapter checklist entries).
  - rf2-jx6y (closed; state-machines case enumerated in Part 1 alongside other optional capabilities).

Status: open. P2 — load-bearing for the multi-impl story (per rf2-vf8m). Action when the spec is closer to lock and the per-spec content has settled enough to enumerate decisions reliably.
close_reason: Created docs/specification/Implementor-Checklist.md as Reference / Companion. Part 1 (How complete?) lists pattern-required core + 7 optional-capability declarations (Q1 machines, Q2 routing, Q3 SSR, Q4 schemas with three-answer split for runtime-schema vs host-types, Q5 stories, Q6 Tool-Pair, Q7 AI-Audit). Part 2 (How achieved?) groups decisions: Foundation (F1-F6), State storage (S1-S3), Subscriptions (Sub1-Sub2), Views (V1-V3), Tracing (T1-T3), Errors (E1-E2), Testing (Test1-Test3), Routing (R1-R2), SSR (SSR1-SSR3), Schemas (Sch1-Sch3), Machines (M1-M4), Tool-Pair (TP1) — each with name, why, options-by-host (CLJS/JS/TS/Python/Rust/Kotlin/Swift), reference-impl picks, trade-offs. Part 3 (Conformance) explains capability-tagged fixture consumption per claimed list. Cross-referenced from 000-Vision §Host-profile matrix, README.md companion-docs index, and conformance/README.md. End-to-end useful artifact pegged to actual current spec content.

title: Eventless :always — drain microsteps formalisation
description:
:always is an eventless transition — fires automatically when its guard becomes true, no event needed. xstate/SCXML term: transient or eventless transition.

## The pattern

A state with :always declares a vector of guarded transitions checked after entry (or after any transition that lands in the state). First matching guard wins.

```
{:checking-form
 {:always [{:guard :form-valid?   :target :submitting}
           {:guard :form-invalid? :target :show-errors}]
  :on     {...}}}
```

## Drain semantics extension

Today Level 3 (within a single machine event):
1. Apply transition.
2. Drain raise-queue.
3. Commit snapshot.
4. Emit accumulated fx.

With :always:
1. Apply transition.
2. Drain raise-queue.
3. Microstep loop: check :always of new state. If matches, apply transition; loop back to step 2.
4. Fixed point reached (no :always matches): commit snapshot.
5. Emit accumulated fx.

The whole microstep cascade commits ONCE, atomically. External observers see only the final settled state — xstate/SCXML macrostep semantics.

## Bounded depth

New error category: :rf.error/machine-always-depth-exceeded. Mirrors :raise depth limit. Default depth: 16 (matching :raise default). User-configurable at frame-config level.

## Trace surface

- :machine.microstep/transition trace event for each microstep.
- Outer :machine/transition event has a :microsteps count in :tags.
- Tools that drill in see the microstep stream; tools that want only externally-observable transitions read the macrostep.

## Interaction with :raise

Within a microstep: drain :raise queue first, then check :always. Combined macrostep is the fixed point of (:raise drain + :always check).

## Interaction with hierarchy

When entering a compound state, :always is checked at every entered level, deepest first. Matches xstate/SCXML.

## Worked example

```
{:initial :asking
 :states
 {:asking
  {:always [{:guard (fn [{:keys [data]} _]
                      (>= (:correct-count data) 10))
             :target :winner}]
   :on    {:answer-correct  {:action (fn [_ _] {:data {:correct-count inc}})}
           :answer-wrong    {:action (fn [_ _] {:data {:wrong-count inc}})
                             :target :loser}}}
  :winner {...}
  :loser  {...}}}
```

User dispatches [:quiz [:answer-correct]]. Macrostep: :correct-count increments → :always check → guard true → transition to :winner. External observers see :asking → :winner; the intermediate "answer counted" state is invisible.

## Locked design calls

1. Default depth limit: 16 (matching :raise).
2. Self-loop :always (state whose :always targets itself with same guard): forbidden at registration time. Reason: gotcha guard against accidental no-op cycles. Error: :rf.error/machine-always-self-loop.
3. Trace events: emit per-microstep events AND aggregate count in macrostep. Tools choose which level to consume.
4. Order with :raise: per microstep, drain :raise queue first, then check :always.

## Schema additions (for rf2-a83)

:rf/state-node gains optional :always slot:
```
[:always {:optional true}
 [:vector
  [:map
   [:guard  {:optional true} :rf/guard-ref]
   [:target {:optional true} :rf/transition-target]
   [:action {:optional true} :rf/action-ref]
   [:meta   {:optional true} :map]]]]
```

## What :always does NOT include

- Mid-transition :always (only state-node key, not transition-spec key).
- :always on root machine (only on state nodes; root has :initial cascade).
- Self-loop :always (forbidden at registration time).

## Conformance fixtures (minimum 2)

1. always-single-microstep.edn — single :always fires after entry; verify single macrostep, microstep count.
2. always-depth-exceeded.edn — cycle of :always transitions; verify error category fires after depth limit, snapshot does not commit, recovery is :no-recovery.

## Files to update when actioning

- 005-StateMachines.md: new §"Eventless :always transitions" near §"Spawning"; update §"Drain semantics" Level 3; update §"Capability matrix" — flip :always from work-in-progress to specified; update §"Drain semantics gotchas" with new gotcha (most common: :always cycle).
- Spec-Schemas.md: add :always slot to :rf/state-node per above.
- conformance/fixtures/: add the 2 new fixtures.
- conformance/README.md: list new fixtures.

## Pairs with

- rf2-a83 (Spec-Schemas additions for v1 WIP capabilities — :always schema closes another piece).
- rf2-3tk (closed; hierarchical states — :always interacts with hierarchical entry/exit).
- rf2-tqv (closed; Circle Drawer audit — Circle Drawer doesnt use :always, no Knock-on).

Status: open. Ready to action — design is locked, just needs a focused agent pass to fold the content into 005 + Spec-Schemas + conformance.

See 005-StateMachines.md §Registration and §Guards.

Schema in Spec-Schemas; two conformance fixtures; two new error categories. Substantive content in 005 §Eventless :always transitions.

title: Add goal: hierarchical FSM substrate with implementor-chosen completeness level
description:
Mike's framing: re-frame2 wants a sufficiently complete FSM-and-actor substrate; implementors choose their capability set. Mike clarified that the actor side is largely done already (spawn, destroy, own state at [:rf/machines <id>], message ports via dispatch/sub-machine, cross-actor send via :fx). Parallel states and history states are explicitly OUT of pattern scope (locked, this iteration) — re-frame2 has clean substitutes for both that didn't exist in xstate's framing.

Reframed as orthogonal capability axes (not tiered levels):

FSM-richness axis (locked targets for v1 pattern):
  - Flat FSM (guards, actions, entry/exit, wildcard :*) — ✓ specced
  - Hierarchical states (compound) — add (main work)
  - Eventless :always — add (small)
  - Delayed :after — add (small; timing semantics need care for SSR/testing)
  - Parallel regions — SKIP. Substitute: separate machines per region, coordinated via cross-actor dispatch. All atomicity, inspectability, and undo benefits ride on the existing single-store machinery.
  - History states — SKIP. Substitute: snapshot-as-value capture (the snapshot at [:rf/machines <id>] is already a value; copy it on leave, restore on re-enter). xstate needs history states only because its runtime doesn't have first-class snapshot-as-value semantics — re-frame2 does.

Actor-model axis (largely already specced):
  - Own state + message ports (actor identity) — ✓ specced
  - Imperative spawn — ✓ specced
  - Destroy — ✓ specced
  - Cross-actor send via :fx — ✓ specced
  - Declarative :invoke (sugar over spawn) — add (trivial; runtime translates :invoke on a state's :on-entry to entry/exit actions that spawn/destroy)
  - SCXML compatibility — out of scope (post-v1, possibly never)

Goal text:
'The pattern anticipates a hierarchical FSM substrate with full actor semantics. Implementations declare which capabilities they support; conformance is graded against the claimed capability list. Parallel regions and history states are explicitly out of pattern scope; documented substitutes (separate machines per region; snapshot-as-value capture) cover their use cases.'

Action items:
1. Add goal to 000-Vision near AI-first amenability and revertibility.
2. Define a §Capabilities matrix in 005, listing each capability with its required prose / schema / fixture coverage.
3. Add §'Substitutes for skipped features' to 005 — documents the separate-machines-per-region pattern (with a worked example like a media player) and the snapshot-capture pattern.
4. Lock the v1 CLJS reference's capability set: all actor capabilities + flat FSM + hierarchical states + eventless :always + delayed :after + declarative :invoke. NOT parallel or history.
5. Update 005's v1-grammar binary table — replace with capabilities matrix; mark parallel and history as 'out of pattern scope; see substitutes.'
6. Conformance corpus: each fixture declares which capabilities it requires.
7. Host-profile matrix in 000-Vision lists each capability as required / recommended / optional / out-of-scope.
8. Worked example: include a media player demo showing separate-machines pattern as a substitute for parallel regions.
9. AI-Audit gets 'capability conformance clarity' graded against whether each spec section names the capabilities it depends on.

Pairs naturally with rf2-5pt (one-shot-implementability) and rf2-tqv (Circle Drawer inspectability audit).

title: Add goal: spec corpus is sufficiently complete that an AI can one-shot the v1 reference implementation
description:
Currently this claim appears only in passing in README.md as a description of what the conformance corpus verifies. It is not stated as a goal in 000-Vision alongside AI-first amenability, frame state revertibility, etc.

Per project memory, this IS the bar Mike has set for re-frame2 ('AI can one-shot the v1 reference implementation'). The bar deserves to be a stated goal because it's a different kind of claim from AI-first amenability:

- AI-first amenability is about design quality from the AI's perspective (regularity, named-things, low hidden context, etc.).
- 'AI can one-shot the implementation' is about the spec corpus's *completeness*. It's the acceptance test for the entire spec effort. If an AI armed only with the spec docs + conformance fixtures can produce a working v1 reference implementation, the spec is done. If not, something is missing.

These are related but distinct. The first is a design property; the second is a meta-property of the spec itself.

Action items:
1. Add to 000-Vision §Goals as a top-level goal. Suggested name: 'AI-implementable from the spec alone' or 'One-shot implementability'. Place near AI-first amenability since it's the natural sibling.
2. Rationale paragraph: this is the acceptance test for the spec corpus. The conformance corpus exists to verify it. Trade-off: forces the spec to be precise where it might otherwise leave details to the implementer.
3. Implications:
   - Every spec must be self-contained enough that an AI doesn't need to consult re-frame v1 source code.
   - Open Questions must be resolved or explicitly bracketed as 'CLJS-reference choice; document your host's choice'.
   - Conformance fixtures must be runnable test cases, not aspirational sketches.
   - Schemas (Spec-Schemas.md) define every shape the spec references.
   - The host-profile matrix names what each host must provide vs what it can choose.
4. Cross-reference from the conformance corpus README (which already mentions the claim).
5. AI-Audit gets a new top-level audit dimension: 'spec self-containedness' — graded against whether each spec relies on external knowledge.
6. Update the existing AI-first principles section if appropriate to distinguish 'amenability' (design) from 'one-shot-implementability' (spec completeness).

Status: open. Worth doing as part of any 000-Vision goal-list pass.
close_reason: Added Goal 2 (AI-implementable from the spec alone) to 000-Vision §Goals near AI-first amenability. Includes rationale, what-this-implies, connection to other goals, failure mode. Cross-referenced from conformance/README.md as the verification mechanism. Goal numbers renumbered (old 2 -> new 3, etc.). New audit row added to AI-Audit.md cross-cutting goals.

description:
AI-Audit flagged Spec 006 (ReactiveSubstrate) as ◐ for the new top-level Goal 'Frame state is fully revertible' (per 000-Vision). The concern: a parallel-substrate adapter could legally put observer/subscription/reaction state *outside* the frame's value (e.g., in a Reagent track-cache, in adapter-private mutable cells), which would mean undo / time-travel / snapshot-restore of the frame value would not fully restore the runtime — observer state would survive the revert.

Add a §'Revertibility constraints on adapters' to 006 making the rule explicit: adapter-internal state used for performance (memoisation, reaction caches) is allowed if and only if it is *derivable* from the frame's value — i.e., dropping the adapter cache and recomputing from the frame value yields equivalent output. title: Document persistent-data-structure dependency for other-language implementors
description:
Re-frame2's design assumes structural-sharing persistent data structures: app-db value-equality is cheap (used by sub-cache invalidation), immutable snapshots are zero-copy (used by undo/time-travel/epoch-history), structural sharing keeps hot-path swaps cheap. For CLJS this is free (Clojure's defaults). For other-language ports, persistent data structures are a strong soft-requirement.

Host implications:
- JS/TS: Immer or Immutable.js; native JS without a library would have prohibitive deep-copy cost.
- Python: pyrsistent / immutables.
- Rust: im-rs (or similar).
- F#/Scala/OCaml: native PDS — zero ceremony.
- Go: requires a library or copy-on-write conventions; a strict idiomatic-Go port would struggle.

Action items:
1. Add a section to 000-Vision (Goals / Pattern constraints) calling this out as a strong recommendation.
2. Add a row to the host-profile matrix in 000-Vision listing 'persistent data structures (PDS)' as a pattern-required capability for dynamic hosts and a 'strongly recommended' for static hosts.
3. List standard PDS libraries per host in Conventions.md or a new Implementor-Notes.md doc.

Status: open. Don't forget to action before any v1-spec freeze.

title: Idea: Declarative subscriptions on a frame (Elm Sub-style) for external event sources
description:
Elm pattern: TEA's `subscriptions : Model -> Sub Msg` — at every step the program returns a *declaration* of which external sources should currently be feeding messages in (a websocket on this URL, an interval at this rate, the keyboard, a port). The runtime diffs declarations across steps and starts/stops the underlying machinery accordingly. The user never starts/stops a websocket — they declare its presence as a function of state. This is the Cmd/Sub *asymmetry*: Cmds are effects you produce (one-shot, fire-and-forget); Subs are message *sources* you currently want.

re-frame2's current position: re-frame's :fx is Cmd-shaped — effects you produce. The 'I want the runtime to feed me messages from source X while condition Y holds' case is currently solved ad-hoc: setup events that start a timer/websocket/eventListener, teardown events that close it, manual lifecycle bookkeeping. Pattern-RemoteData §Polling shows the workaround using :dispatch-later self-recursion. There is no first-class declarative subscription concept on a frame.

Why investigate: this is the missing half of the effect vocabulary. Concretely: a :subscriptions slot on reg-frame returning data — `[[:interval 1000 [:tick]] [:ws "wss://..." {:on-message [:msg]}] [:keyboard [:key-down]]]` — diffed each drain, with the runtime starting/stopping :sub-id-shaped sources. Solves websockets, intervals, keyboard listeners, document.visibilitychange, server-sent events, IntersectionObserver, and similar — which today are leaky setup-event patterns prone to forgotten teardown on frame destroy. Big AI-amenability win: the AI reads one declaration to know what's listening, not a scatter of setup/teardown events.

Fit: stays inside the closed effect model — :subscriptions is *declarative*, the runtime translates to an internal start/stop on registered subscription handlers (a new kind alongside :event/:sub/:fx). Frame-scoped lifecycle is automatic; :on-destroy stops everything declared. Hard constraint check: NO core.async — diffing is plain values, fire-and-forget callbacks dispatch events. Multi-frame check: each frame has its own :subscriptions slot.

Risks: registry-kind growth (a new :sub-source kind). Mitigation — could be modelled as a special idiom over reg-fx with explicit start/stop semantics rather than a new kind. Worth careful design — the asymmetry Cmd↔Sub is a deep idea and getting it wrong wastes the slot.

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
close_reason: Rejected exploration: does not fit the intended re-frame2 direction.

title: Idea: register the :assert/* event vocabulary as a public, enumerable assertion DSL
description:
Source: Storybook's @storybook/test exposes a small, named assertion vocabulary (within/expect/userEvent) that is deliberately a tiny surface — easy to learn, easy for AIs to generate. Storybook play functions are just sequences of those calls.

re-frame2's current position: 007-Stories.md §Play functions sketches :play [[:auth/email-changed ...] [:assert/path-equals [:auth :state-machine] :authenticated] ...] but does not enumerate the :assert/* vocabulary. The current text mentions :assert/path-equals as an example without committing to a list.

Why worth investigating: per Principle 'Public query surfaces' and 'Named things over anonymous things', the assertion vocabulary should be a *registered* set of events whose ids are enumerable via (rf/handlers :event) (filtered by :assert/ prefix). Concrete candidate vocabulary: :assert/path-equals, :assert/path-matches (predicate), :assert/sub-equals, :assert/dispatched? (event was dispatched during play), :assert/no-warnings, :assert/state-is (machine), :assert/effect-emitted. AI scaffolding (CP-10) would query the registrar for the :assert/* prefix and pick from the enumerable set rather than guessing names.

Fit/risks: lives in the post-v1 story library — these are story-tool-supplied events, not framework primitives. Risk: registering :assert/* events globally collides with user namespaces; mitigation is a reserved :rf.assert/ prefix. Cleanly composes with 'story-as-test duality' — same vocab works in :test mode (assertions fail loudly) and :dev mode (rendered as a checked-step list).

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
notes: Actioned: added 'Assertion vocabulary as a registered, enumerable DSL' note to 007-Stories.md §Play functions, with the candidate :rf.assert/* vocabulary. Bead remains open — vocabulary needs to be locked in alongside the post-v1 stories library.
close_reason: decision: :rf.assert/* is a reserved namespace (Conventions.md); the post-v1 stories library registers the canonical vocabulary at load time (path-equals, path-matches, sub-equals, dispatched?, state-is, no-warnings, effect-emitted); AI scaffolders enumerate via (rf/handlers :event ...); edit: docs/specification/007-Stories.md, Conventions.md

title: Idea: derive :argtypes from registered schemas (Spec 010) instead of hand-writing
description:
Source: Storybook 8 auto-derives argTypes from TypeScript types / JSDoc / propTypes, so authors rarely write the control-type table by hand. Histoire does the same from Vue prop definitions. Result: controls panel 'just works' once the component is typed/schema'd.

re-frame2's current position: 007-Stories.md §Argtypes describe controls requires the variant author (or AI) to hand-write {:argtypes {:placeholder {:control :text} :variant {:control {:type :select :options [...]}}}}. This duplicates information already present in Spec 010's view :spec / arg schemas (a Malli enum becomes a :select; a string becomes :text; a boolean becomes :boolean; a number with :min/:max becomes a number control with bounds).

Why worth investigating: pure AI-first win. The view already declares its argument shape via Malli (per Spec 010); auto-derivation removes a class of hand-written boilerplate where the AI is just transcribing schema → controls. Also: a single source of truth for arg shape — schema drift between view and argtypes is impossible.

Fit/risks: adds a 'malli → argtypes' resolver to the post-v1 stories library — no v1 framework hook needed. Risk: not every Malli shape has a clean control mapping (recursive schemas, multi-spec variants). Solution: auto-derive when possible, allow manual override for the rest. Fits 'post-v1 library scope vs v1 framework hooks' cleanly: lives entirely in the stories lib.

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
notes: Actioned: added 'Auto-derivation from Spec 010 schemas' note to 007-Stories.md §Argtypes describe controls. Bead remains open — Malli→argtypes resolver design needs detail.
close_reason: decision: auto-derivation from Spec 010 schemas locked as principle (post-v1 library composes the resolver); inline note in 007 §Argtypes upgraded from 'under investigation' to 'locked principle; resolver post-v1'; edit: docs/specification/007-Stories.md

title: Idea: CP-10 — Construction Prompt for stories/variants/workspaces
description:
Source: Storybook CSF3 (story-as-data with declarative meta), devcards (cards-as-forms), Histoire (story-file-as-component). All have AI-friendly scaffolding shapes; CSF3 in particular is what AI agents converge on when writing Storybook stories.

re-frame2's current position: Construction-Prompts.md ships CP-1..CP-9 (event/sub/fx/view/machine/feature/route/schema/SSR). There is no CP for the story/variant/workspace artefact. 007-Stories.md positions reg-story/reg-variant/reg-workspace as post-v1 sugar but stories ARE one of the AI-first surfaces (they encode 'a component in a known state' as data — high-value AI input).

Why worth investigating: construction prompts are a 'deliverable principle' (Principles.md). Stories are arguably the highest-leverage AI deliverable (story-as-test, story-as-doc, story-as-agent-input — see 007 §Story-as-test duality). A CP-10 template would (a) preflight-check the parent view is reg-view'd; (b) preflight-check the events fired in :events are registered; (c) emit reg-story + N reg-variant forms with a documented :tags default; (d) cross-link CP-4 (view), CP-1 (events), CP-8 (schema for argtypes). Brings stories into the same construction-prompt regularity AI tooling expects.

Fit/risks: CP-10 is documentation, not runtime; sits cleanly with existing prompts. Risk: stories are post-v1 library, so CP-10 is forward-looking; can be marked 'CP-10 (post-v1)' and shipped when reg-story/reg-variant land. No constraint conflicts.

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
notes: Actioned: added a 'Construction prompt (CP-10)' sketch section to 007-Stories.md and a forward-reference in Construction-Prompts.md header. Bead remains open — full CP-10 template lands when re-frame.stories ships.

title: Idea: Pending-navigation state in app-db so views can render loading UI
description:
(a) Source ecosystem and pattern: React Router v6/v7's useNavigation exposes navigation state ('idle' | 'loading' | 'submitting') so any view can render a global progress bar or pending UI without manual bookkeeping. TanStack Router exposes isFetching/isLoading per route. Remix's pending UI story is one of its headline features.

(b) What 012 currently has: 012's :route slice is {:id ... :params ...}. There is no notion of 'a navigation is in flight,' no place a sub like :route/pending? or :route/transition can read from. Consumers wanting a progress bar would have to roll their own coordinated flag in app-db, which is exactly the kind of hidden context AI-first wants to avoid.

(c) Why investigate: real SPAs need pending UI. SSR-driven first-load also has a 'hydrating' moment that views may want to know about. A tiny addition to the :route slice — :transition with values like :idle / :loading / :error — and a registered sub :route/transition would make this a one-liner for views and an enumerable property for AIs. Especially powerful when combined with declarative loaders (rf2-5tf): the runtime knows when route-level fetches start and finish.

(d) Fit/risks: fits public-query-surfaces (named, queryable, deterministic). Plays well with state-machines (003/005) — :transition is itself a tiny FSM. Risks: if the runtime doesn't know what 'finished loading' means without declarative loaders, the application has to manage :transition itself, which is little better than a hand-rolled flag. So this idea is most powerful if rf2-5tf lands; otherwise leave it as a documented convention.

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
close_reason: decision: ship :transition (:idle | :loading | :error) and :error in the :route slice; sub :route/transition and :route/error. Runtime-driven (set :loading while :on-match drains, :error if any errors). Spec edited at 012-Routing.md §The :route slice, §Reading the route is a sub; Spec-Schemas.md §:rf/route-slice.

title: Idea: Canonical machine snapshot persist/restore for SSR and Tool-Pair time-travel
description:
(a) xstate concept and concrete value: getPersistedSnapshot / restoreSnapshot are first-class — a snapshot serialises to JSON, reloads, and the machine resumes at the right state with context intact. xstate v5 enforces serialisability of context for this reason. Used for SSR hydration, replay, and dev-tools.

(b) re-frame2's current position: :rf/machine-snapshot is defined as a value shape (Spec-Schemas), and 011-SSR's hydration payload carries app-db. But there is no explicit contract for what 'a machine snapshot survives the wire and resumes correctly' means — e.g., context functions are forbidden? in-flight transition microstate? 002's epoch records also store db-before/db-after, which already brings machines along for the ride.

(c) Why worth investigating: the spec gets persistence almost for free because machines live at app-db paths — but 'almost' hides issues. If a child machine was mid-transition (waiting on an HTTP reply event), what's persisted? If a transition table version changes between snapshot and restore, what then? Tool-Pair epoch replay (rf-three-ai-layers) hits the same questions. A small named contract (snapshot-stable invariants, version tag, restore semantics) would lock these down.

(d) Fit / risks: aligned with closed effect-map, no new substrate — just clearer semantics on existing shapes. Could ship contract in v1 (stability rules) and tooling post-v1 (machine-snapshot-version / migrate-snapshot). Risks: adding a version field to the snapshot shape pressures the closed-shape principle; consider :meta-only.

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
close_reason: decision: locked machine-snapshot stability rules — print/read round-trip, no in-flight microstate, stable across re-registration, optional :rf/snapshot-version under :meta; restore = replace-app-db-at-path semantics shared by SSR hydration and Tool-Pair epoch restore; edit: docs/specification/005-StateMachines.md §Machine snapshot stability, Spec-Schemas.md §:rf/machine-snapshot

title: Idea: Declarative per-route data requirements (loader-equivalent) on reg-route
description:
(a) Source ecosystem and pattern: React Router v6/v7, Remix, TanStack Router, and SvelteKit all colocate a route's data dependencies with the route definition (loader / +page.server.load / loader fn). The route declares 'this view needs X data'; the framework runs that loader on URL match (server and client) and the view consumes the result. Nested loaders compose; route-level revalidation is a first-class concept.

(b) What 012 currently has: 012 mentions a route->fetch-effects helper and a per-route-id multimethod as the conventional pattern; data fetches are emitted as ordinary :fx by :route/handle-url-change. There is no first-class slot on reg-route describing the data the route needs, and no enumerable surface telling tools 'these are the fetches associated with :route/cart'. CP-7 likewise leaves it implicit.

(c) Why investigate: AI scaffolding and tooling can do dramatically more if a route's data dependencies are declarative rather than buried in a multimethod. Declaring :fetch [[:cart/load-items] [:user/load-prefs]] on reg-route makes 'what loads when this route mounts?' enumerable via handler-meta, runs identically server- and client-side (matches goal #3), and lets a tool render route-loading dependency graphs. Compiles down to the existing :fx pipeline — no runtime change. Touches rf2-0fj.

(d) Fit/risks: strong fit with public-query-surfaces, named-things, and data-before-magic. Closed effect-map is preserved (the :fetch slot is metadata, not effects). Risks: revalidation semantics (when do we re-fire?), conditional fetches, parameterising the fetch by :route/params — these need a small DSL; do not over-engineer.

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
close_reason: decision: ship :on-match as a vector of event vectors that the runtime dispatches on URL match (server- and client-side). Re-fires when params/query change; doesn't re-fire on hydration. No new effect substrate; pure event-and-fx. Spec edited at 012-Routing.md §Per-route data loading; CP-7 updated.

title: Idea: Model-based testing harness over machine-transition (xstate/test analogue)
description:
(a) xstate concept and concrete value: @xstate/test generates test cases from a machine — paths, coverage, shortest-path-to-state — by treating the machine as a graph. The pure transition function makes this cheap and the generated tests are exhaustive in a way handwritten cases never are.

(b) re-frame2's current position: 005 ships a pure (machine-transition definition snapshot event) → [next-snapshot effects] in v1. CP-5 demonstrates handwritten path tests. Nothing in the spec proposes generating those tests from the table.

(c) Why worth investigating: the highest-leverage, lowest-cost feature xstate has and a near-perfect AI-first match — the table is data, the transition fn is pure, an AI can ask the harness 'cover every transition' and get an EDN fixture corpus back. Plugs directly into the conformance corpus story (Spec-Schemas §Conformance). Can ship as a separate testing helper without touching the runtime.

(d) Fit / risks: zero conflict with machines-as-event-handlers, no core.async, no new effects — the harness reads transition tables and calls the pure fn. Risks: defining the coverage model (state-coverage vs transition-coverage vs guard-coverage) is non-trivial; effectful actions (HTTP) need stubbing in the harness. Naturally slots into the post-v1 library, but the v1 transition contract is already enough to build it externally.

Status: exploratory — needs investigation, not yet a directive.
notes: Documented as forward-pointer in docs/specification/008-Testing.md §Future and 005-StateMachines.md §Future (post-v1 library item — sketch surface: rf/test/machine-paths, rf/test/shortest-path-to). Needs Mike's call: lock the API surface in v1 (so post-v1 library is constrained) vs leave fully open (post-v1 library defines its own API)?
close_reason: Design locked: post-v1 library 're-frame.machines.test'; transition coverage as default; :after timers via explicit time-advance using re-frame.interop test-clock; auto-stub fxs in test mode with opt-in recursive coverage of spawned children; EDN-fixture output in corpus shape. Spec-side acknowledgment landed in 005 §'Model-based testing harness — re-frame.machines.test' documenting the substrate guarantees the harness relies on: pure machine-transition, data-only tables, machine-scoped guards/actions as fns, conformance corpus shape. Library work post-v1; v1 substrate is sufficient.

title: xray: investigate pre-existing test:xray-feature-gate failure — 'multi-frame isolation substrate' (epoch-panel focus timing)
description:
Discovered during rf2-bufw2 / PR #2395. The worker reported `npm run test:xray-feature-gate` fails on the 'multi-frame isolation substrate' case — an epoch-panel focus timing issue. CONFIRMED PRE-EXISTING: the worker re-ran the gate on a throwaway worktree at clean baseline 7f1f93234 and got the identical failure, so it is NOT introduced by rf2-bufw2.

Why it did not block #2395: test:xray-feature-gate runs in .github/workflows/expensive-tests.yml:82 (nightly/release sweep), NOT the PR test.yml workflow (test.yml:1327 comment confirms the full sweep is excluded from PR time). So PR CI is unaffected; the nightly/release gate is the one at risk.

Investigation steps: (1) Check the most recent nightly expensive-tests workflow run — if it is GREEN there, the failure is a Windows-LOCAL timing/focus flake (env-specific, lower priority; the worker ran on Windows). If RED there, it is a genuine regression on the multi-frame epoch-panel focus path needing a fix. (2) If real, root-cause the epoch-panel multi-frame focus timing and stabilise. Surface: tools/xray epoch panel + multi-frame isolation testbed. Cross-ref: rf2-bufw2, PR #2395 worker report.
notes: FIX SHIPPED: PR #2396 (https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/2396). Awaiting merge (worker does not merge). Gates green: test:xray-feature-gate 14/14, xray clojure -M:test 964/0, fast PR spine PASS. Follow-on rf2-5fyo3 filed for the SEPARATE Story nightly failure that is the actual cause of the red expensive-tests nightly.
close_reason: Resolved via PR #2396 (merged). The xray 'multi-frame isolation substrate' failure was a DETERMINISTIC test-gesture bug (3/3 repro): the gate focused a cross-frame cascade by dispatch-id WITHOUT first re-targeting Xray onto :counter/b, so the single :epoch-history slot (keyed to :target-frame) wasn't re-seeded and the Epoch panel rendered the wrong frame's head. PRODUCTION IS CORRECT — fixed test-only (15 lines, scenarios.cjs) by adding setXrayTargetFrame before the focus, mirroring the canonical user gesture + the passing CLJS e2e analogue. test:xray-feature-gate 14/14 green. RE-BUCKETING: the chronic nightly expensive-tests redness (05-21->05-27) was MISATTRIBUTED to xray in this bead's original triage — it is actually a STORY failure (test:story-feature-load aborts the set -euo pipefail block before test:xray-feature-gate runs); now tracked + in-flight as rf2-5fyo3. Also noted on prior bead notes: a separate '20-event launch-mode' flake under concurrent load (passes solo) — not fixed.

title: spec/014 §Privacy: 'privacy at a glance' paragraph mapping four entry points to owning namespaces
description:
Per rf2-6kd3u ruling (Mike 2026-05-29 option A): the HTTP privacy surface stays split across three implementation namespaces (re-frame.http-privacy / http-privacy-headers / http-url) because the structural seam is real — headers and URL params are different decoration surfaces.

  - clear-sensitive-headers!      (owner: re-frame.http-privacy-headers)
  - declare-sensitive-query-param! (owner: re-frame.http-url)
  - clear-sensitive-query-params! (owner: re-frame.http-url)

  2. The composers (http-privacy ns) get a one-sentence mention as the orchestrating surface.

title: xray Reactive panel: retire SUB VALUES section (kept flow diagram)
description:
Per Mike pair-debug 2026-05-29: the Reactive Panel (Views tab) carries a SUB VALUES section that lists each cached sub's current value via the edn-inspector. With the Epoch panel's SUBSCRIPTIONS table now surfacing per-cascade sub values + per-sub diff chrome, the SUB VALUES section duplicates the same information without the Epoch context.

Mike's call: retire the SUB VALUES section. Keep the reactive-flow diagram (the view→sub→app-db graph) — that's the unique-to-this-tab signal.

## What changes

### `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/reactive_panel_view.cljs`

Three regions go:

1. `(sub-values-section data)` call at ~L682 in the panel's render path.
2. The `sub-values-section` defn at ~L572-595 (the section wrapper + the rows render).
3. The per-row helper `sub-value-row` (or similar) at ~L524 — the row-level renderer for one sub's id + value.

The ns docstring's SUB VALUES bullet at ~L36 retires alongside.

Kept under the same panel:

- `flow-graph` (the reactive-flow diagram) — the unique-to-this-tab artefact Mike wants to keep.
- `unmounted-views-section` — different concern (lifecycle), keep.
- `destroyed-subs-section` — different concern, keep.
- `legend` — keep.

### `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/reactive_panel_subs.cljs`

Whichever sub computes the `:sub-values` slot on the data the panel reads — retire it (the sub-id + the slot's writer if separate). The reactive-panel's other slots (flow-graph data, unmounted views, destroyed subs) stay.

If the per-sub value lookup is shared infrastructure (e.g., used by the popup-on-row affordance elsewhere), it stays — only the section-level summary projection retires.

### Registry snapshot

`tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/registry_cljs_test.cljs` allowlist — remove any `:rf.xray.reactive/sub-values` (or equivalent) sub that was registered solely to feed the retired section.

### Tests

`tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/reactive_panel_view_cljs_test.cljs` (or equivalent) — any test that asserts the SUB VALUES section renders / its data-testids are present / the rows route through edn-inspector retires. Tests for the flow-graph + lifecycle sections stay.

### Spec

`tools/xray/spec/<reactive-panel-spec>.md` (or `spec/021-Dynamic-Panel-Designs.md` §Reactive panel) — remove the SUB VALUES section prose. The reactive-flow diagram remains the spec's anchor for the panel.

## Acceptance

1. Reactive panel renders the flow graph, unmounted-views, destroyed-subs sections — no SUB VALUES section visible anywhere.
2. `git grep -nE "sub-values-section|SUB VALUES" tools/xray/src` returns ZERO matches.
3. Registry snapshot test passes (no orphan sub registration for the retired feed).
4. Tests for the retained sections (flow graph, lifecycle) keep passing.
5. spec/021 prose updated.

## Scope

Single-file dominant: `reactive_panel_view.cljs`. Sub registration touch + spec prose. Single PR. Pre-alpha — no shim.

## Rationale

The SUB VALUES section was the right call before the Epoch panel surfaced per-sub values (rf2-e46qs phase 3, originally rf2-oqa60 phase 3). Now the Epoch panel's SUBSCRIPTIONS table — with FULL+DIFF rendering, per-row sub values, the `← was X` annotation (rf2-fyd8u in flight) — covers the same information cradled in the cascade context. The Reactive tab's value-listing is duplicate inventory.

Pair-debug 2026-05-29.
notes: Retired the Reactive panel's SUB VALUES section. PR #2381 (worker/xray-reactive-retire-sub-values-rf2-uz3wm). Net -584 LOC. All gates green: tools/xray (957 tests), implementation cljs (4831 tests), mkdocs --strict, slug/readme checks, clj-kondo.

title: refactor(test-support): consolidate trace-recorder helper across adapter test trees
description:
Naming audit rf2-5r7eh observed file-local divergence across adapter test trees for the same trace-recorder pattern: every test ns that wants to capture a stream of trace events defines its own near-identical `defn- <verb>-traces[!]` helper that wraps `trace-tooling/register-listener!` with an atom.

Reagent adapter occurrences (rf2-5r7eh):
- events_cljs_test.cljs            collect-warnings
- cross_spec_dom_cljs_test.cljs    collect-traces + stop-traces
- frame_provider_context_dom_cljs_test.cljs    collect-traces + corruption-traces
- sub_dispose_view_cljs_test.cljs  collect-dispose-traces!
- write_after_destroy_cljs_test.cljs   collect-traces! (returns {:traces :stop!} map)
- render_key_cljs_test.cljs        record-render-traces!
- view_render_trigger_handler_cljs_test.cljs   record-traces!
- view_rendered_op_cljs_test.cljs  record-traces! + record-by-op!
- view_side_capture_cljs_test.cljs record-op!

The verb (collect- vs record-), the ! suffix, and the return shape (bare atom vs map) all diverge. The sibling adapter slices (uix, helix, reagent-slim) very likely carry the same pattern.

Proposed fix: extract a single `re-frame.test-support/with-trace-recorder!` (or similar) helper. Suggested shape: takes a predicate selecting the events of interest + optional listener-key, returns a {:traces atom :stop! fn} map. Every per-file defn is then a 3-liner OR is deleted entirely. Cross-adapter parity emerges for free.

Scope: cross-cutting refactor across implementation/core/test-support/ + implementation/adapters/{reagent,uix,helix,reagent-slim}/test/. ~10 callers, mostly mechanical.
